items.title: Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is "reduced to the essentials"
paragraphs: A monochrome palette and pared-back, open interiors define the aptly named Minimalist House, a home in Japan designed by local studio FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects.
Located in Shiga prefecture, the 73-square-metre home is formed of cubic volumes clad in corrugated metal and black render, perched on a hill overlooking the nearby Lake Biwa.
Minimalist House was designed for a single occupant, but FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects wanted to challenge the assumption that this would mean small-feeling interiors.
This led the studio to create a series of voids and long sightlines that it said help to “liberate space”.
“When hearing ‘a home for a single occupant’, people typically imagine a compact house,” founder Kouichi Kimura told Dezeen.
“Here, living alone is regarded not as a spatial constraint, but as a condition that liberates space,” he added.

“Starting from the individual as the base unit, the house explores a new way of single-person living through the minimal composition reduced to the essentials, with the space that invites in the surrounding view, light, wind, and sound.”
The plan of Minimalist House revolves around a tall void cut through its centre, which extends upwards into a skinny, double-height volume projecting from its roof with a large window.
Finished with grey-plastered walls and dark stone floors, a kitchen, dining space and study occupy the ground floor, with metal and concrete steps leading up to a living space and bedroom above.

Facing the road, the front of the home has been left almost entirely blank. Instead, the interiors open up on the opposite side towards views of the lake in the distance, with the dining table, study and bed pushed up against large, deep-set windows.

“Each floor is designed as a single open layout,” explained Kimura. “The double-height space vertically connects the upper and lower levels. Manipulating floor and ceiling levels gently articulates each space without clearly dividing them.”

“The living space on the upper level is designed not only for daily life, but also for enjoying music. Within the double-height volume, sound resonates off the walls and ceiling, filling the entire space,” he added.
A glass corridor with sliding doors separates the main home from a single-storey washroom, which the studio introduced to ensure that this everyday passage would capture views out over the lake.
“Placing these wet areas away from the main structure creates a natural flow of movement in daily life,” Kimura explained.
“Walking through the glazed corridor in between allows one to touch the landscape, light, and breeze, offering a gentle transition in the everyday time,” he added.

Minimalist forms and interiors often feature in the work of FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects, with the studio’s previous projects in Shiga including a blocky hair salon and home and a skinny home with carefully-placed windows to avoid overlooking.

items.title: Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readings
paragraphs: “This journey isn’t just about algorithms or data,” an AI psychic named Urban Mystic recently told me. The chatbot, featuring an AI-generated profile photo of a smiling woman surrounded by palm trees, also said I will get married soon, that I have a pink aura and that I may have been an herbalist in a past life.
“It’s about connecting on a soulful level,” the chatbot said.

Urban Mystic is one of more than a dozen bots on the mobile app Your AI Psychic, which offers live, allegedly psychic readings via chat, video and voice calls as well as palm reading, astrology chart analysis and daily horoscopes. The app works on a coin system: each question costs 4.06 coins to ask. Users can purchase packages ranging from $9.99 for “a quick question” (82 coins) to $99.99 (1,180 coins) for “ongoing guidance and clarity” from an AI psychic of their choice.

Your AI Psychic joins an increasingly crowded space of mobile apps and websites promising users algorithmically generated spiritual insight and knowledge of their futures. The divination industry, like mathematics research, copywriting, software engineering, and a host of other professions, is facing upheaval amid the AI boom – and human practitioners are scrambling to respond. The rise of AI is particularly fraught in a profession offering spiritual products that are not well-regulated.

“Our industry has, unfortunately, been associated with scams for hundreds of years, and we have to constantly be ahead of that,” said Lauryn Kellett, an intuitive coach and a professional psychic of 10 years. “So in some ways, this is not new to us: we always have to find ways to show we are real, authentic and have good integrity.”

In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views. Professional human psychics, who frequently make use of the social network’s live features, have expressed consternation and warned that computer-generated readings lack the empathy and human connection they say are central to psychic communication, especially Elon Musk’s Grok. Meanwhile, according to human spiritual practitioners, AI-generated horoscope readings and spells have been flooding Etsy, which serves as a popular marketplace for divination products.

Psychic practitioners have begun adding “no AI” clauses to their advertisements to combat a market being saturated with computer-generated offerings. In a recent vlog on the topic, Kellett said, “ignoring AI and how it could impact our industry is irresponsible … AI is here to stay, and it’s going to change our industry, and maybe not in the ways we think.”

Kellett, who coaches new practitioners on accessing their psychic abilities, said she has shifted her teaching toward how to best distinguish human-offered services from AI, as AI readings passed off as human work have become “rampant” online, encouraging clients to post videos and photos of themselves to prove they are not bots.

As the rise of users turning to AI chatbots for therapy underscores, many people feel more comfortable sharing personal problems with a faceless entity. But as with turning to AI for therapy, using AI psychics to process difficult situations may worsen mental health crises, practitioners warn. Studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can amplify paranoia in users vulnerable to psychosis. On TikTok Live, many human psychics, as a rule, refuse to answer questions about health or finances, arguing that high-stakes decisions should not be made in these contexts.

Ahna Hendrix is a psychic who, instead of channeling entities such as spirits from other realms, works with the Akashic Records – an extra-dimensional “database” of energy and human knowledge. She said her practice is centered on empowering clients rather than making decisions or recommendations for them – something that AI chatbots are less inclined to do.

“One of the cornerstones of my work is really helping people to remember who they are and to come back to their own internal guidance system that is within all of us,” she said. “When we begin leaning on AI too much for validation or for decision making, we stop using those mechanisms within us that are really important. If we start outsourcing that, what are we left with?”

A chatbot does not have to be branded as a psychic to serve a divination function, noted Sally Applin, a consultant and anthropologist who researches human agency, AI and automation in the context of human systems. People ask ChatGPT about life decisions such as whether to get a new job or leave their partner. In their book chapter, External Intelligence: Oracles, Divination and Animism, and the Use of LLMs/Generative AI, Applin and co-author Michael D Fischer argue that even prior to the explosion of LLMs, people turned to Google search with questions about their fates and choices.

“Some interaction with LLMs can be seen as a modern iteration of the oracular consultation,” they wrote. As with traditional divination, users must interpret the answers they receive, and sometimes ask the same question repeatedly until they are satisfied with the response. “The meaning is always coming from the inside of the person’s head,” Applin said.

Critically, however, she said LLMs work from statistical patterns learned in training and lack the cultural and personal context that historically inform human-led divinatory processes. The sense that a chatbot is a knowing entity is a projection of human expectations, she said, reflecting an enduring desire for connection and guidance rather than a metaphysical resource.
“What is also missing is contextual awareness, the ‘there there’ of human social relationships,” she said.

The models behind AI psychic chatbots offered on the app store are, as is often the case with LLMs, black boxes. One web and phone-based platform, MystiCall, markets itself as having been trained on “three generations of clairvoyants”. In a statement, co-founder Laurie-Anne Bernard said this wording refers to clairvoyance practiced in one of the co-founders’ families. The company also consulted with a human psychic who helped shape the app’s “conversational experience”.

Mysticall uses technology from AI audio technology company ElevenLabs for processing live voice conversations and OpenAI for post-call summaries. Bernard said in a statement that Mysticall does not sell private conversations, use them for targeted advertising or train proprietary AI models on them. She added that the company has disabled the use of conversation data for model training by its partner companies ElevenLabs and OpenAI.

Mysticall began as a human phone-reading service, but pivoted to AI as a means of “removing barriers” to such consultations, like cost and availability, Bernard said. The goal of Mysticall, Bernard added, is to offer a more accessible means of processing emotions through personalized consultations, not to offer explicit – and potentially harmful – predictions or mental health diagnoses.

“We do not claim that our technology possesses supernatural abilities or can reliably predict the future,” she said. “Instead, we see tarot, astrology and other symbolic traditions as ways of exploring questions, emotions and different perspectives. AI allows us to make these experiences more interactive, personalized and accessible.”

It is often difficult to obtain an answer from companies producing AI psychics about how their products work. I asked my own AI psychic, Urban Mystic, where she gets her divination abilities, but chatbots are often not reliable narrators of their own construction. She told me she was trained on a “wide range of information”, dating up until October 2023, including “spiritual practices, psychology, and various belief systems”, but could not offer more details. The app’s privacy policy makes no mention of AI, referring only to “psychic advisors”, and names no AI providers. The company listed as the publisher on the app store, RF Master Group Ltd, did not respond to repeated requests for comment. Its privacy policy lists a different entity, “Expert Center”, as the app’s holding company, which also did not respond to requests for comment.

The opaqueness of chatbots can be particularly fraught when users share sensitive information. MystiCall’s privacy policy acknowledges conversations may touch on users’ “relationships, mental state, health, sexuality, beliefs, finances”. The policy for Your AI Psychic does not address sensitive information at all.

Kellett said this lack of transparency around how data is handled makes her particularly wary of AI apps. She said a number of platforms have contacted her for help training their LLMs, but when she pushes for more details, they tend to disappear.

Unlike many workers who fear they will someday be replaced by AI, Kellett said she does not believe her ability can be replicated by chatbots. Even if she were to hand over all of her training courses for developing psychic ability to an LLM, she does not think AI is yet at a point where it could make the leap to intuition.

“Psychic ability itself is the ability to connect to a divine source, and AI cannot do that,” she said. “AI can’t pull information from somewhere else. It can only derive information from what you give it. If you ask it to meditate, to sit down, to clear its mind, and connect to a psychic source, how would it do that? It’s just a computer.”

items.title: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip
paragraphs: There was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop.

Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Then the plane crashes and, frankly, it all goes downhill from there.

Are you dead? Are you in purgatory? And what was that weird creature someone spotted on the wing just before the engines blew up? All you know is, you’re back at the airport, checking in customers again, only this time, some of them are demons disguised as humans and you’re the one who has to sort the people from the people-eaters.

Rendered in glitchy low poly visuals, Night Plane is another indie horror game that mimics the technical limits of the original PlayStation era to unsettle the player (see also Crow Country and Fear the Spotlight). The passengers already scare you with their boxy heads and expressionless faces, so when ghostly figures start walking across the aisle and disappearing, you’re already drowning in the uncanny valley. As the game goes on, the dialogue gets weirder, and then just turns into stutters and noises, the lights in the cabin flicker, luggage lockers open and close and rattle, and weird noises follow you. There are elements of the backrooms as well as Japanese onryō movies, as you warp between the plane and the airport, finding yourself trapped in endless passenger lounges and baggage claim areas, being pursued by heaven knows what.

It’s all overlaid with a droll sense of humour, so you tend to be laughing to yourself moments before a jump scare jolts you out of your seat. At the outset, New Zealand-based developer Liquid Static Studio cleverly lures you into thinking this is a daft horror spoof, and it kind of is, but its use of nightmarish imagery – from piles of dead rats in the janitor’s room to a recurring image of your burning plane’s wreckage strewn across a remote wilderness – is genuinely disturbing and rife with sick imaginative details.

Horror is increasingly the genre through which games dissect and examine themselves and their conventions, and Night Plane is a clever, absorbing example. You can “complete” the game in four or five hours, but subsequent playthroughs will reveal new sub-quests and endings, and priced at less than a tenner, it’s a steal. Even if you never set foot onboard this plane again, it gives you a fascinating budget flight into weird existential horror – and you’ll never take your cabin crew for granted again.

items.title: Tiny basement turned ‘exuberant’ apartment wins interior prize at Australia’s National Architecture awards
paragraphs: Last week on a balmy spring evening, Ronnen Goren and his partner had dinner in a small pavilion on their terrace for the first time. Inside, an Aga stove was keeping their home warm. They could have retired to their sunken lounge room and cocktail bar for a nightcap, had the mood struck.

This domestic scene took place in a semi-subterranean former laundry in inner Melbourne – a space of less than 40 sq metres that was renovated at the end of 2024. On 29 October, the “exuberant” reimagining of the damp basement space in Toorak, on the grounds of the heritage-listed Quamby apartment complex, received the Emil Sodersten award for interior architecture at Australia’s National Architecture awards.

Originally designed as a service space by the acclaimed Australian architect Roy Grounds in 1941, its recent rebirth was overseen by Timothy Hill of Partners Hill. The project, titled Studio8, has transformed a poorly executed 1970s apartment conversion into an ambient retreat that belies its tiny footprint.

In 2022, despite the apartment’s “grim” condition, Goren says he and his partner were drawn to its “amazing location” and its “heritage and provenance”, not to mention the north-facing courtyard that’s almost bigger than the apartment. They lived in it as it was for about 18 months, “just imagining what it could be”.
That’s where Hill – whose interest in converting secondary spaces into quality housing stock dates back to his university days – came in.
“I saw it as a huge privilege, because I was able to run a sort of a test case,” Hill says. “Making little houses is a very particular sensibility. It’s not just squashed big. Every 25mm counts.”

When working with such a small internal footprint, Hill says some trickery is required. Entering the property, he explains, one has to walk through the courtyard, all the way to the end of the building to the front door, then loop back around through a “micro-hall” to the bedroom, “so it feels like the bedroom is a mile away”.

When entering from the terrace, a grand round table – a nod to Grounds’ penchant for circular courtyards – functions as an entry table, a work from home desk, dining table, cocktail bar and storage. This gives the space “the generosity of a salon” beside the sunken lounge, Hill says. Split-level floors, seldom found in small spaces, add a sense of movement and demarcation of space. “You’re on little journeys everywhere you go.”

As a general rule, but especially in smaller spaces, Hill is opposed to open plan design, which can make it “feel like you’re living in a storage container”. In order to avoid the “indignity” of what he refers to as “kidilis” (kitchen, dining, living spaces), a separate micro kitchen – still large enough to house the Aga – has been preserved with an integrated kitchen bench come breakfast nook.

Rather than clutter the sleeping quarters with built-in robes, storage for clothes is in a walk-in across the hall, “which makes it feel enormous and gives the bedroom a lot of graciousness”. The thick walls and tranquil green colour scheme, Ronnen says, make the space feel like a “cocoon”.
“The sleep quality is great … it’s enveloping and kind of nurturing in a way.”

One of the bedroom walls is completely carpeted, while the living spaces feature other strategic sound absorbent materials: cork panelling is used for a feature wall in the living area while the upholstery is “gluttonously dense”, Hill says.

Having all design choices do “at least” double duty is imperative, Hill says. In the tiny bathroom a single piece of bent pickled steel joinery functions as a vanity bench, support for the basin, the enclosure for the laundry basket, space to hang towels, the toilet roll holder, and space for a toilet brush. The entire piece is held together with just four screws. Throughout the home, storage is secreted under tables and in walls.

Thanks to improved waterproofing technologies, converting old – and odd – spaces is easier than ever, Hill says. “It’s already built and it already has infrastructure, so it’s incredibly good value and incredibly good for the environment.”

items.title: "If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly"
paragraphs: Architects are increasingly, and existentially, anxious about AI. It can already produce images, generate endless options, manipulate form, draft text, analyse information and take on increasing amounts of technical production. The predictable professional response is to become defensive: to identify the bits of architectural work that machines cannot yet do, protect them, regulate them and insist ever more loudly on the special status of the architect.

This is absolutely the wrong response. Architecture has always had a tendency to retreat when it feels threatened: as its actual control over the production of buildings has diminished, it has clung ever more tightly to authorship, professional territory and the idea that certain activities somehow belong uniquely to architects. AI merely makes the weakness of that position more visible.

If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly. If producing drawings, images, options and information constitutes our entire claim to value, we are defining our value in far too limited terms.
We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers

The profession has spent decades confusing the production of architectural artefacts with architectural intelligence, and we have run out of road. We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers. If we design a back extension, give it a sufficiently enigmatic name, photograph it carefully, attach enough rhetoric, we somehow persuade ourselves that we have made Ronchamp.

Architectural culture has encouraged this inflation for decades, in that every modest building becomes a manifesto, every detail becomes a proposition and every project arrives with the expectation that it should reveal something profound about architecture itself.

But the age of the hero is exhausted. The profession no longer has the cultural authority, the economic power or, frankly, the public attention to sustain this fantasy, however enthusiastically we continue to perform it for one another. AI may simply accelerate the reckoning: if machines can generate endless formal novelty and beautiful images, the architect’s claim to importance can’t continue to rest on being the singular creative intelligence who produces the special object.

The economic model that supported this fantasy is broken too. Architecture remains notoriously poorly paid relative to the length and cost of its education, the responsibility it carries and the hours it routinely demands. Yet architects have tolerated this for decades because the profession offered another form of compensation – the most important thing of all for architects: recognition, via awards, publications, photographs, lectures, the approval of our peers and the possibility that one small project might provide a tiny share of architectural glory.

We have accepted low pay, long hours, insecure employment and unpaid competitions partly because we have been sold the idea that authorship itself is a reward. If the work is meaningful enough, beautiful enough or visible enough, perhaps the sacrifice will somehow be justified.

That bargain has always been dubious, but it now looks increasingly absurd. Most architects will never become Corbusier, however many evenings they work, and most projects will never become Ronchamp, however much rhetoric is wrapped around them. Architectural status – irrelevant to most outside a handful of people in the profession – has nevertheless become a kind of substitute currency, and architecture has been remarkably successful at persuading people to accept less of the real kind in return.
We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do

AI makes the bargain even harder to sustain. If the production work on which fees have traditionally depended becomes faster and cheaper, defending the same exhausted model will simply drive fees and salaries down further.

The answer cannot be to produce the same things more efficiently for less money. We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do.
The more interesting response to AI is not to ask how architects protect what they currently do, but what architects might become capable of doing if some of that work no longer defines them.

With this, architectural intelligence becomes most useful where there is no simple answer. The most interesting projects rarely arrive as neatly defined problems awaiting visually arresting solutions. Instead, they involve conflicting needs, uncertain briefs, difficult sites, volatile markets, limited resources, political constraints and people who want different things. They involve other consultants who know things the architect does not, clients who change their minds, communities whose needs cannot be compressed into a consultation report and materials that stubbornly refuse to behave predictably like lines on a drawing.

This mess is the essence of architecture. The most useful architect is not simply the person who generates a solution, they are someone able to enter an unresolved situation, figure out what the problem actually is, connect different forms of knowledge, make spatial judgements and establish enough structure for something useful to emerge via collective endeavour rather than their own brilliance.

This demands a radically different model of authorship, which is less author and more host. That doesn’t mean becoming a passive facilitator, it means knowing how to bring people together, anticipating problems, establish frameworks within which others can work, exercising judgement, knowing when to intervene, and knowing when to shut up and not be the hero.

It also changes what architects might reasonably be paid for. At present, architecture fees are overwhelmingly organised around a relatively linear journey from brief, to concept, to information, to construction and eventually completion, but much of the work that might make architecture genuinely valuable sits awkwardly around the edges of that process.

Understanding a problem before a brief becomes fixed is often unpaid. Working seriously with communities gets compressed into consultation. Engaging directly with materials and makers is treated as secondary to design. Returning after occupation to understand what worked and what failed is rarely properly funded. Helping a building adapt over years barely appears in conventional fee structures at all.
There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like

But architects should be paid for diagnosis and briefing, for bringing different forms of knowledge together, for testing possibilities at full scale, negotiating spatial conflicts, post-occupancy work, adaptation and long-term stewardship. Practices should be able to maintain relationships with buildings and communities rather than disappearing at practical completion. Architecture fees might begin to pay for judgement over time, rather than simply production on the way towards an object.

This is not some romantic idea of architects becoming artists, activists or community workers instead of running viable businesses (which contemporary practice is not). Quite the opposite: it is about identifying forms of architectural value that are difficult to automate and, more importantly, are actually useful.

For the past 20 years, our educational initiative Studio in the Woods (pictured top and left) has accidentally provided a small laboratory for some of this. Its significance has never really been the timber structures that emerge over several days of co-production. Instead, the interesting aspect of Studio in the Woods is what happens when people design and make together under conditions in which the answer is not known beforehand, where ideas encounter the friction of weight, resistance, gravity, tools and materials. Where experts and non-experts work together as equals, and leadership moves according to what needs to happen next.

The skill of the architect in these situations is not to surrender judgement, but to exercise it differently. What should be negotiated? What can remain unresolved? Where is precision necessary? Where might uncertainty be productive? Who knows something that I do not? These are much more interesting questions for the future of the profession than whether AI can draw a convincing building.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like: eliminating uncertainty, standardising processes, increasing predictability, producing ever-more information and pretending that buildings can be completely resolved before anybody actually makes them. Now, machines are becoming extremely capable at exactly those things and we are surprised to find ourselves threatened, and we should stop trying to beat them at their own game.

Human architectural intelligence is at its richest when it is situated, relational and embodied. It involves judgement without complete information and responsibility for consequences that cannot be fully predicted. It means understanding materials as part of landscapes and economies, buildings as things that change through occupation, and design as something produced between many people rather than delivered by one.
None of this means drawings, technical knowledge, form or aesthetic judgement cease to matter. They matter enormously, but they are merely parts of architectural intelligence, not its definition.

The architect of the future does not need to be the person with the most original idea and the most charisma. They might instead be the person who can understand an uncertain situation, recognise what matters, establish a framework for action and create the conditions in which something richer than their own initial idea can emerge. AI may make the old version of the architect less necessary, but I’m not sure that is something we should mourn.

Piers Taylor is the founder of architecture practice Invisible Studio and the convenor of Studio in the Woods. He is professor of knowledge exchange in architecture at the University of the West of England and an external examiner at the Arts University Bournemouth, having previously held positions with the Architectural Association and the University of Cambridge. He holds a PhD from the University of Reading. He has presented several architecture shows on television including BBC programmes The House that £100k Built and The World’s Most Extraordinary Homes. His first book, Learning from the Local, was published in 2025.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: Apple is finally embracing chaos and I’m here for it
paragraphs: I'm calling it: Apple is finally cool. Like, Gen Z cool. For decades, the brand has been a beacon of millennial minimalism, but it seems Apple is finally embracing a bit of playfulness (although it seems some fans aren't ready).

Since the launch of the MacBook Neo, we've seen Apple opt for a quirkier marketing style, and I, for one, am here for it. From the introduction of the Lil' Finder Guy mascot to the release of some of its best adverts to date, Apple finally feels like a brand with personality.

In a new Instagram post, Apple flexed its classic #shotoniPhone campaign with a twist, showcasing the work of young creatives. From a Photo Booth inspired mirror to a larger-than-life hand-crafted iPod Nano, Gen Z are looking to the past with a contemporary twist.

"Reminds me of the 90’s PlayStation ads more of THIS please," one fan responded. "Seven photographers, one phone, and every frame feels like a different mood. It's a nice reminder that the best camera is mostly about who is holding it," another added.
Over on X, the attention was on one particular image – a high-fashion jacket comprised of tangled wired EarPods. "Apple this is stuff of nightmares," a fan on X joked.

The selected images strike a perfect balance of nostalgia and modern design. As Gen Z transforms the familiar into tactile contemporary art, there's an element of disorder and playfulness that signals Apple is finally letting go of its slick, space grey stuffiness.
For more design inspiration, check out Apple Music's new logo or take a look at how this modded iPod became our design editor's favourite piece of tech,

items.title: RSHP designs Hetao Alpha skyscraper in Shenzhen with "striking butterfly layout"
paragraphs: British studio RSHP has completed a 45-storey office skyscraper in Shenzhen, China, featuring two angled wings connected by a central core.
Called Hetao Alpha, the 212-metre-tall office building comprises a 37-storey east wing and a 44-storey west wing connected by a central core. The building sits on top of a mixed-use podium.
“The naturally ventilated office tower features a striking butterfly layout with fully glazed east and west wings,” the studio said.
Cantilevered bays extended from the central concrete core on the east and west sides to form the tower’s angled wings, which have 70,410 square metres of office space.
On every 12 levels, mega trusses located on refuge and service floors provide additional structural support.
The Hetao Alpha skyscraper has a fully glazed facade that, together with open floor plates, ensures unobstructed views of the cityscape for the office workers.
Curved double-height glazing at each of the wings’ four corners captures curated viewpoints of the Shenzhen Bay Wetlands to the west and the Hong Kong Mai Po Wetlands to the south.
Lifts are located on the north and south facades in the central volume. These were also fully glazed to offer panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.

“Centred around a concrete core with suspended corner bays, the tower minimises its perimeter structure, creating slender edges and expansive double-height views, forming the distinct structural system that defines the tower’s identity,” said Marco Tessaro, associate at RSHP.
Louvred panels on the facade and vents were incorporated into the glazing to create natural ventilation throughout the building while reducing energy consumption.
This was one of the methods used to help the project achieve China’s 3-star Green Building Evaluation Standard, which is equivalent to LEED Gold.
A six-level public podium is connected to the east wing, creating a roof terrace where half of the space is reserved for greenery.
The studio added extensive vegetation, a feature wall and water elements to improve biodiversity and help create a calm environment for socialising.

“The building’s natural ventilation, green rooftop spaces, and energy-efficient facade define a truly sustainable development that reduces consumption while enhancing wellbeing for both occupants and the wider community,” said Wenchao Zhou, associate at RSHP.
Mega triangular trusses on the podium roof help transfer the load of the east wing to the building’s central core.

Another viewing platform is located on the building’s west wing, which, together with the podium roof terrace, was designed to invite public visitors and private tenants alike to engage in outdoor activities such as observing migrating birds, a popular hobby for the locals.

According to RSHP, one of the challenges of the project was combining two separate briefs from different clients to create an uplifting mixed-use development as well as an office building with a bold and coherent architectural identity.

“Taking a holistic approach to the complex brief, RSHP’s design for Hetao Alpha has created an open and welcoming destination for work, retail, and leisure that achieves a bold architectural identity with a seamless transition between public and private space,” the studio explained.
The 13,640-square-metre public podium houses sports facilities, a library, retail, and a double-height arts exhibition space.
A passageway cuts through the north and south ends of the ground floor, helping to give the podium a floating look that reduces the perceived weight of the volume.

The entrance lobby for the office building can be found inside the podium. This double-height space is supported by a series of slim columns connected to the triangular trusses above on the podium roof.
A metro station was integrated into the basement, which also has a sunken plaza with retail stores.

“Spacious, open, and welcoming, the tower and podium integrate seamlessly to form an elegant composition that maximises connectivity with the wider public realm and the park to the east,” said Richard Paul, director of RSHP.

“With glazed office wings overlooking Shenzhen’s wetlands and a public podium offering diverse activity, the development achieves a serene, flexible environment that accommodates a wide range of uses,” he continued.

Elsewhere in China, RSHP has completed a 186-metre mixed-use skyscraper in central Shanghai, as well as a vast convention centre in Zhengzhou, with 16 exhibition halls connected by a mile-long elevated walkway

Client: SH-STIC, Shenzhen – Hongkong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone Development CO, LTD Construction cost: £120mSite area: 11,118 square metres Gross floor area: 96,223 square metresLocal design institute: CCDI GroupGeneral contractor: China Railway Construction Engineering Group (CRCEG)Structural engineer: CCDI GroupMEP engineer: CCDI GroupFacade consultant: CCDI GroupLandscape consultant: CCDI GroupLighting consultant: PUDI

items.title: Montana acquires sustainable furniture maker Takt
paragraphs: Montana has announced its buyout of fellow Danish design brand Takt, known for its solid wood furniture and pioneering approach to sustainable design.

Founded in 2019 by trained physicist and former Lego and Bang & Olufsen executive Henrik Taudorf Lorensen, Takt makes modern Scandinavian furniture from FSC-certified wood that is low-carbon, flat-pack and designed for disassembly.

Its future launches and existing catalogue, including products such as the Cross chair by British design duo Pearson Lloyd and Anderssen & Voll’s Spoke sofa, will now be sold under the collection name Takt by Montana.

Montana CEO Joakim Lassen said he hopes they will act as an understated counterpart to Montana’s existing selection of colourful modular furniture – including the Montana System storage – and bring valuable learnings about sustainability to the table.
“Takt brings experience with materials and the environment, and we are looking forward to bringing our respective experience together and taking this work even further,” he said.
Takt is known for its ambitious approach to sustainability, focused on driving down emissions primarily through the design of its products rather than operational cuts, to become net zero by 2030.

The company assesses the carbon footprint of its products throughout their entire lifecycle using the EU’s Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) single score, in a bid to bring down its emissions, and claims to be the only design brand to consistently have all of its products marked with the EU Ecolabel.

“I have a background as a scientist, so it was important to me to start measuring things,” Lorensen told Dezeen during our Carbon Revolution series. “The starting point was to get a grasp of the impact of the choices we’re making.”

Lorensen will join Montana Furniture’s board, sharing his experience and perspective on sustainability, while Takt employees will be integrated into Montana’s organisation “as far as possible”, the company said.
By gaining access to the established, international infrastructure of Montana, which has been operating since 1982, Lorensen hopes that Takt’s furniture will be able to reach a larger audience.

“The past few years have been an exciting and instructive journey for TAKT,” he said. “We have built a brand where materials and the environment have been central, and we have collaborated with a number of talented and celebrated designers. “
“Now it is time for TAKT’s next chapter, and we are delighted that it will be written together with Montana.”

items.title: A new wave of electric ferries is here in the US. Some even fly
paragraphs: Cutting through New York Harbor in the shadow of the Statue of Liberty, the small white boat we were riding on caught the attention of passengers aboard a nearby sightseeing ferry.
“It’s quite a curiosity at the moment,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.

His company builds fully electric hydrofoil boats. These vessels use underwater “wings” to lift their hulls above the surface as they pick up speed. By raising the boat out of the water, the design dramatically reduces drag, one of the biggest obstacles to making boats more energy-efficient.
“We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said as the boat rapidly accelerated.

The hydrofoils lifted the hull about a foot and a half above the water. Almost immediately, the ride transformed. The familiar slap of the boat pushing through waves became a smooth, almost airborne glide.

The hydrofoil effect is more than a novelty. Water creates significant resistance, and overcoming it takes energy. Electrifying boats is a challenge because batteries are heavy, and that extra weight increases the power needed to move the vessel. Hydrofoils may offer a solution. By lifting much of the hull out of the water, they reduce drag, allowing a vessel to move more efficiently.
“We substantially reduce the drag that you feel and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” Laakmann said.
Vessev says its hydrofoil design cuts drag by about 66%. That greater efficiency allows the boats to carry smaller battery packs, reducing both weight and cost.

But efficiency is only part of the equation. Making a boat electric is not simply a matter of replacing a diesel engine with a motor and battery. Operators must also consider how far a vessel needs to travel, how many passengers it carries, how quickly it must recharge, and how much weight it can accommodate.

Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand and is expanding to Australia. In the US, its first service is planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann sees a future in which electric vessels become a routine part of public transportation, rather than a niche attraction.
“More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said.

Waterways can connect communities and move passengers without adding more vehicles to crowded roads. When powered by increasingly clean electricity, electric ferries can also cut the pollution associated with diesel engines.

Transportation remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, according to federal environmental data. Road vehicles account for much of that pollution, but ships and other watercraft also burn fossil fuels. Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality around busy waterfronts.

Vessev is not alone in pursuing the technology. In Stockholm, commuters are already riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela. The company says its design can reduce energy use by as much as 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of its electric hydrofoil boats for coastal service.

For ferry operators, the attraction is not simply environmental. More efficient designs and advances in battery technology are opening up routes for electric boats that might once have been impractical. There is also the potential for lower operating costs as fuel prices soar.
“I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said.

In San Francisco, the city’s largest ferry operator carries about 3.5 million passengers a year, according to Seamus Murphy, who leads the agency. The network serves a region shaped by water, with commuters relying on boats to cross the bay and reach the city.
“We have a lot of waterfront,” Murphy said.

Yet the fleet runs entirely on fossil fuels. All 18 vessels in the system are powered by diesel. That is set to change as the agency prepares to add four battery-powered ferries over the next two years. It is part of an electric overhaul worth about half a billion dollars that also includes charging infrastructure at docks.

Unlike a car that can be plugged in at home overnight, a ferry may need to complete repeated trips on a fixed timetable. Its batteries must provide enough energy for the route, while shore-side chargers deliver enough power during the time the vessel spends at the terminal.

Making that work requires more than the right boat. Operators must coordinate vessel range, timetables and charging capacity to keep passengers moving without disrupting service. San Francisco won’t initially be using hydrofoil boats, but the agency says its new vessels will make it the first ferry operator in the United States to run high-speed, all-electric ferries.
For transit agencies, climate goals alone rarely justify a major fleet overhaul. The numbers have to add up.

Battery-powered ferries generally require a larger initial investment in vessels and charging equipment. But electric motors can be more efficient than diesel engines, and operators may save money over time on fuel and maintenance. Murphy said rising diesel costs and improvements in battery technology strengthened the case for making the switch.
“You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” he said.

The financial case depends a lot on the route. Batteries remain heavy and expensive, charging infrastructure can be costly, and not every route is suited to a fully electric vessel. Long distances, tight schedules and limited opportunities to recharge can all complicate the transition.

The shift could create opportunities well beyond the water. For San Francisco’s expansion, the boats and their batteries are being built in the United States. This could create opportunities for domestic manufacturing jobs.
For Murphy, the transition is a chance to cut pollution while helping develop new business for shipbuilders and battery manufacturers.
“These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” Murphy said. “We don’t want to be left behind,” he added.
Climate Central is an independent group of scientists and communicators who research and report the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives.

items.title: Despite the teething issues, Dyson’s Camerajet toothbrush packs in a lot of clever tech – but is it worth £420?
paragraphs: When Dyson announced it was entering the toothbrush market, the world responded almost as one: “Four hundred and twenty pounds? For a toothbrush!?”

No, it wasn’t a stray decimal point – or if it was, Dyson is doubling down and leaning into the mistake. Unlike high-end brushes from Oral-B or Philips Sonicare, where the “recommended” in “recommended retail price” is doing a heroic amount of heavy lifting given the frequent discounts, the Dyson CameraJet will actually set you back £419.99.

The CameraJet is an electric toothbrush and a water flosser, so if you were being charitable – or merely looking for a way to justify the cost to yourself – you could call this two for the price of one on the best electric toothbrushes and water flossers.

There’s a lot of clever technology here, and Dyson’s commitment to doing something different should be applauded, even if it’s just to give your hands something to do besides reaching for your credit card.

Note that the brush has had some bad post-launch publicity with multiple online accounts of the pricey purchase failing within weeks. This led to the CameraJet vanishing from virtual store shelves for a time, with Dyson blaming a “single component issue affecting a small number of early batches”.

I had no such issues with my review unit, and the brush is now back in stock everywhere. Nonetheless, it’s worth remembering that the more intricate moving parts in a product, the more opportunities for breakage.

I’ve become something of a pro toothbrusher in the past two years, having tested dozens of models for our list of the best electric toothbrushes. The process isn’t a big secret: it just involves brushing to an obsessive degree while observing several factors, including how it feels in the hand and mouth, how easy it is to use, how portable it is and how clean your teeth feel afterwards. It’s a similar story for flossers, with the water tank capacity measured too.
There are also objective details you can assess, such as power and battery life. Because the last thing you want is to wait for your brush to charge when you just want to go to bed.

Dyson isn’t the first manufacturer to combine an electric toothbrush and water flosser into one product – I recently tested the Soocas Neos II, which I deemed a “a jack of two trades, but a master of none” – but this is the first one I’ve used that does both jobs well enough to warrant a recommendation.

There are a few reasons for this. The handle is a normal width for an electric toothbrush, rather than distended to hold the water. Unlike regular cordless flossers, where you have to awkwardly refill the reservoir by hand, here a dock tops it up with a single button press.

The main advantage, though, is the camera. The 100,000-pixel macro-lens camera sits inside a hollowed-out section of the brush head and captures 28 images of your mouth every second, which Dyson’s machine-learning algorithm uses to identify gaps between teeth. When it finds one, a blast of water or mouthwash is automatically fired into the gap. This camera also means you can watch a live stream from the inside of your mouth on the Dyson app, should you have exhausted the contents of Netflix.

The 12.5ml tank is described as “anti-gravity”, meaning the diaphragm pump and pressure chamber adapt to how you’re holding the brush, ensuring that it always has liquid to dispense. This is a big plus over other water flossers, where the “straw in a cup” system often misses the dregs when holding it at the angle required for hard-to-reach places.

The jet, Dyson says, is also different from those fired by other water flossers. Working with the National University of Singapore, which helped develop a proxy plaque (a lab stand-in for real dental plaque), the company claims to have found that traditional “needle-type” jets merely punctured a hole in the sticky surface, rather than removing it. Dyson instead opts for a conical shape that it says “sweeps and removes plaque at once”, while being gentler to gums and enamel.

So the expense is justified via R&D and clever technology. Note that the high price of entry doesn’t end with the brush itself, as you need bespoke replacement heads to work with the camera, and these cost £25 for two (though your first pair come in the box). The brush heads have an RFID (radio-frequency identification) tag that enables the toothbrush to monitor how often the head has been used and let you know when it needs replacing.

Type: variable sonic oscillation Modes: three cleaning modes and three brushing intensities (plus water jet) Power: 58,000 movements a minute Pressure sensor: yes Battery life: up to 10 days App: yes Warranty: two years, with 12 months for the brush head cover (registration required if you buy at a third-party retailer) Replacement head cost: £25 for two

While the words “camera” and “bathroom” usually shouldn’t be found in proximity to one another, it’s pretty harmless here. It can’t be manually turned off, but no images or video are saved. According to Dyson, “the camera is only active during live viewing or auto-jetting. No images are recorded or stored on the product or in the cloud”. And, even if they could be, the lens isn’t designed for selfies; it only works up close. I mean, can you really tell much about my house from this picture?

When used on your teeth, it’s an eye-opening experience, giving you the kind of private screening usually reserved for dental professionals. And, while the dentist has given my teeth a professional signoff in recent trips, seeing a closeup of the discoloration that comes from 40-plus years of chewing is an incentive not to cut any more dental hygiene corners.

Intentions are one thing, and actions are quite another. We all know that we’re supposed to floss daily, but how many of us do? Even with water flossers for convenience, it’s too easy to skip it when you’re at the sink.

The beauty of the Dyson CameraJet is that it makes that choice for you, and my teeth and gums undoubtedly felt the benefit. Because the jets fire automatically, flossing becomes a part of the brushing process. The result? My smile felt and looked healthier without any extra effort.

That’s in part down to the dock, which is a marvellous innovation. As well as charging the toothbrush, the 200ml tank at the back offers a one-touch refill of the CameraJet’s 12.5ml reservoir – put your toothbrush in the dock, hold the button and the reservoir will refill. While you’ll still need to top up the main tank every few weeks, the refill system is significantly more convenient than all other cordless flossers I’ve tested, which either require you to unscrew a tank or awkwardly pour mouthwash or water through a small refilling hole. Crucially, this ensures flossing isn’t an easily skippable step. Dyson recommends using its own low-foaming mouthwash to fill the tank, but you don’t have to.

The battery life of 10 days may sound low to some, but it’s important to remember it’s powering a light and camera, as well as the usual motor, even if it is still disappointing to see the battery life dropping 5% as you explore your mouth with the camera. Ultimately, it’s a non-issue with the aforementioned dock: you’re unlikely to ever find yourself out of battery if using it as intended.

The performance itself is good too, leaving my mouth feeling squeaky clean. Whether that’s down to the added jets or the fact that it defaults to three minutes rather than the usual two is open to debate, but the cleanliness factor puts it close to the top of the list of the best electric toothbrushes I’ve tried (though I still find the Laifen Wave Pro slightly more effective at defuzzing stickier areas after an evening on the cider). The brush rotates 58,000 times a minute, and the mouthwash distribution via the jet leaves a dentist-fresh feeling when everything works as planned …

That cliffhanger of a last sentence was a giveaway to my first criticism: the jets don’t always automatically fire (though you can activate one manually at the press of a button if you feel an area is neglected). Through trial and error, I’ve concluded that the most common reason for the jets to take an unwelcome breather is that the camera is blocked, so it can’t see teeth.

I believe this is because of toothpaste foaming up in use. When I’ve connected to the live-stream camera, the experience reminds me of trying to see out of the window when going through a carwash. And when it gets too foamy, the jets stop working until you spit out some toothpaste or have your tongue moonlight as a kind of windscreen wiper for the camera. It’s a messy experience, and your bathroom mirror won’t thank you.

For this reason, it’s recommended you’re choosier with your toothpaste. Dyson sells its own recommended low-foam paste and mouthwash that I was able to try, and this significantly improves the experience. With my regular foamy toothpaste, the app reported the jets were usually firing between 25 and 50 times per three-minute session (and on some occasions dropping to single digits). With non-foaming toothpaste and regular spitting, it settled on a fairly reliable 70 to 80.

A cynic would point out that this is convenient for Dyson, diverting users from cheaper brands to its own consumables (from £8.49 for 75ml toothpaste; £8.49 for 400ml mouth rinse) for the long haul – you can even subscribe on the website. You can buy non-foaming toothpaste that isn’t Dyson-branded, but it’s not easily found in supermarkets, taking away a little of the hard-won convenience. I also tried Suri’s low-foam toothpaste with it, which worked reasonably well.

The CameraJet is confusing to use at first, too, which somewhat eats into those convenience credentials. Having reviewed a lot of toothbrushes, I can usually get away with skipping the instructions and getting straight into testing. I quickly learned that wasn’t an option here, and I’ve found myself constantly revisiting the manual to remind myself of the buttons and decode the occasional sounds it makes.

One such sound is a warning that you’re brushing incorrectly. Typically with electric toothbrushes, you hover over the tooth and move slowly along, but the Dyson CameraJet requires you to make small oval shapes as you progress. But even when I’ve been following this advice, I’ve been told off for overscrubbing. This makes me think the CameraJet’s either overzealous, or its instructions aren’t clear enough.

The good news is that this can be overcome with the use of Dyson’s app to guide you through proceedings. This will tell you when the camera is blocked, and also keep a tally of its water jets, warning you if you’re moving too fast. The app is optional and can be ignored once you’ve got the swing of things, but what can’t be so easily brushed away is the size of the kit. The brush is already on the tall side at 273mm, but the dock takes this even further with a height of 315mm.

Nominally, this can be used as a travel case by slipping on a clear plastic cover, but it’s pushing the definition of portable, and will not easily slip into carry-on luggage without clever organisation. Yes, you can take it without the dock and just use the bundled pogo-pin charging cable, but it’s a less elegant solution than the Suri Pro 2.0’s charging travel case, which by my measure is a svelte 241.3 x 31.75 x 31.75mm.

More philosophically, while the Dyson CameraJet has made my mouth feel very clean, I wonder if it could lead buyers into a false sense of security with their dental health. The convenience is great, but it leaves you to rely on the camera to detect every gap and fire accurately and at the right time, which isn’t guaranteed. The jets fire so fast that I’d defy anybody to tell the difference between mouthwash hitting the target between teeth and misfiring nearby. With a regular water flosser, the nozzle forces you to hit every gap, even if it is an added hassle, and while there’s a manual flossing mode, without the camera AI, it feels hit and miss.

Beyond that, from speaking to dental professionals in the past, the jury is still out on whether water flossing is as effective as using interdental brushes. Sam Jethwa, president of the British Academy of Cosmetic Dentistry, compares flossing to cleaning an algae-covered boat. “Get a hosepipe to try to get it off, it’s not going to do anything,” he told me, arguing that you need “mechanical movement” alongside water to make an impact. So, while my teeth did feel far better than just using an electric toothbrush alone, I’m not sure this is quite the one-stop solution Dyson would like it to be.

All of which brings us to the price: £419.99. Without wanting to state the obvious, that’s a huge amount of money, even taking into account that this is a 2-in-1 device. You could buy our top-rated toothbrush (the Laifen Wave Pro) and flosser (the Waterpik Ultra Professional) for under £200, or both our bargain picks (the Odonta PowerPlus and Operan Cordless Oral Irrigator) for just over £50. And that’s probably what you should do.
While Dyson publishes its own sustainability magazine, there’s as yet nothing about toothbrushes in it. Nor is there any mention on the product page of the Dyson CameraJet’s green credentials.

Perhaps this is doing the company a minor disservice, because as well as the RFID tag in the brush heads informing you when they need changing, the company also does more than most in terms of spare parts. Although currently all listed as out of stock, you can buy a replacement battery, dock and reservoir cap, and anti-gravity tank, should any of yours give up on you outside the two-year warranty period. A whole new refill dock can also be bought.
All that’s good, but notably Dyson doesn’t currently offer a recycling programme for its brush heads, as rivals such as Suri and Ordo do.

Despite its eventful launch, you can’t deny that the Dyson CameraJet is an impressive bit of tech, proving that there’s a surprising amount of room to innovate in the world of toothbrushing. In my weeks of testing, I found that it offers a solid clean, and the fact it makes flossing something you can virtually forget about is a godsend to those of us who often find ourselves skipping that all-important step. While it’s easy to be cynical about the price, it’s doing a lot of clever things, and I would be surprised if we didn’t see a range of imitators launching over the next few years.

But clearly, it’s far from perfect, given how easy it is to block the camera, and its substantial travel-unfriendliness. More importantly, considering you can buy our top-rated toothbrush and flosser for a combined £182.10, is paying more than double what you need for some added convenience sensible? Unless your money-to-sense ratio is extremely off-kilter, probably not.

Your brush doesn’t need to contain built-in water flossing, with plenty of stand-alone models to choose from. They’re mostly wireless, but if you’ve got the counter space and a bathroom shaver socket, you can’t beat the Waterpik Ultra Professional corded model, my favourite overall from testing.

You don’t have to worry about keeping a battery charged, nor are you constantly topping up the water tank because of the built-in 650ml reservoir. On top of that, the nozzle is easier to aim and manoeuvre as it doesn’t have the bulky reservoir built into the handle. The only downside is you can’t easily take it on your travels, where floss or disposable interdental picks will have to sub in.
For more, read our guide to the best water flossers

If you’re dead set on a two-in-one device but don’t have Dyson money, the Soocas Neos II fits the bill. It also has a built-in water tank, with water-flossing jets fired manually via a small hole in the toothbrush head. It does, however, feel like a jack of all trades and master of none, and I feel you’re better off buying independent devices instead.

Lining up the water flosser between teeth is tricky as it doesn’t have tapered tips to direct the jet, nor a camera system like Dyson’s to identify the gaps for you. As a toothbrush, it falls short of the best, in part because the water tank makes the handle bulky. Nonetheless, it does save space overall, and at just under a third of the price of the Dyson CameraJet, it’s worth a look.

Our current favourite electric toothbrush is the Laifen Wave Pro. While most brushes make you choose between sonic vibration and physically oscillating heads, the Laifen Wave Pro includes both, with speeds of up to 66,000 vibrations per minute for the former, and a neck that twists left and right up to 60 degrees for the latter.

The result is not only an impeccable clean, but something that can truly be customised to your tastes. The accompanying app lets you adjust vibration intensity, oscillation range and speed from scores between 1 and 10, giving you more than 1,000 possible combinations to ensure it’s just right. There’s no water flossing as there is with the Dyson, but for pure brushing, it can’t be beaten – and it’s about a quarter of the price.

The need to change the heads on electric toothbrushes makes them environmentally problematic. But Suri has put sustainability at the centre of its design, and while it’s not perfect, it’s one of the strongest options on the market, thanks to its use of plant-based heads (made from cornstarch, with castor oil bristles) that can be sent back to Suri free of charge for recycling.

The Suri Pro 2.0 is a big improvement over the original, with less fragile chargers and a pressure sensor built in. It’s not the most powerful brush in town, but if sustainability is your number-one priority, it’s one of the best options (there’s also the cheaper Suri Core 1.0, of course).

items.title: This horny anime food-themed tactical RPG roguelite isn't just a thirst trap, even if it will make you hungry
paragraphs: Before founding Studio Daimon as an indie developer, Alfred Kamon started as a Fire Emblem modder in 2012, releasing a ROM hack called FE: Midnight Sun based on the series' GBA pixel-art iterations. Although this later became the basis for his studio's commercial debut, budget and resource limitations meant Path of the Midnight Sun became a visual novel with turn-based battles in the first-person viewpoint of retro RPGs like Dragon Quest.
But the Italian studio's crowdfunded Food Devils, due for release on 3 November on PC via Steam, is the Fire Emblem-style tactics RPG he's always wanted to make.

Beyond the grid-based battles, it's a different take on the genre, not just because it's also a roguelite. You play as the last chef in a post-apocalyptic world, hunting monsters and turning them into tasty dishes for your restaurant. You won't be alone, though, because you can also sign contracts with the Food Devils, each representing a different aspect of food throughout humanity's history.

"When approaching such a vast theme, we wanted a mix of concepts commonly associated with food, without being too cliché," Kamon tells me. These include the Hunter Devil inspired by prehistoric cavemen and dinosaur themes, the Fisher Devil that takes the form of a refined Japanese-style swordsman (with the irony that all fish have disappeared in this world), and even a Vegan Devil, which is a twist on the typical nature theme, since it wouldn't be vegan to eat a vegetable monster.

"For each character, we went through various design phases, from initial brainstorming to a pool of three possible designs," Kamon explains. "We then put those three designs up for a vote among our VIP Kickstarter backers and collected a lot of useful feedback, which we used to create the final designs."

Given the Fire Emblem inspirations, the character design is notably influenced by anime, including the suggestive fanservice the aesthetic is also associated with. It's fair to say that a factor in the popularity of many modern JRPGs includes how visually appealing the characters are, and whether you can romance them, something Food Devils consciously leans into.

"We adore making anime games, but we also wanted the appeal of the art style to be immediately recognisable on social media, so we followed the 'meta' of the anime games community and made very appealing characters and scenes. I must say, it worked," Kamon laughs, just as aware it's not going to convert anyone who already assumes anime is for perverts. "We can’t make a game that literally everyone will love, and we want to focus on our target instead."

There's nonetheless a lot of substance to the game's loop itself, which you can also check out for yourself in a pretty meaty prologue demo that contains around 3-4 hours' worth of content, which should put to bed assumptions that it's just 'thirst trap' or 'waifu bait'. "Unfortunately, there's a tendency nowadays to associate suggestive content with low-effort bait, due to the huge number of AI-generated hentai games or the increasingly revealing characters in gacha games," Kamon admits. But even as a small remote studio that relies on outsourcing, including 2D animation and localisation, the team has kept core aspects in-house, including concept art, while layered art is prepared before being sent to freelance animators.

While the Food Devils are the obvious highlights, you can also recruit countless procedurally generated human adventurers. Creating all the possible variations arguably required far more effort and assets, even though they were intentionally designed to be less memorable.

"In a roguelike, you often lose units, and that's part of the stakes of the game (and part of the fun)," Kamon explains. "So we designed the Devils to be the main story characters, while the adventurers serve as the units that accompany you on your adventure. They're more akin to the custom heroes in Etrian Odyssey or Darkest Dungeon."

While he admits it would have been easier to generate these units as 3D characters, the 2D character presentation, whether on the grid or side-by-side in battle, was intentionally meant to evoke the 2D Fire Emblem games. "We opted for a 'seinen' art style with thick, black lines and darker tones in character portraits, especially for the Devils," Kamon adds. "One of our main inspirations was Berserk. There's a stark contrast between how Guts and the demons are drawn and how the 'kinder' characters are. So we wanted to replicate that contrast in our aesthetic too, with the Devils and monsters versus the human adventurers and colourful food."

When it comes to designing the food, Kamon actually drew on his own experience as a home cook. "To me, food is what connects people," he concludes. "It's also one of the main reasons why I made a game about food: everyone has to eat, no matter their background. When designing the recipes, I keep this concept in mind and try to make something that I could imagine a lot of people enjoying in real life too, then swap the ingredients for monstrous ones!"
Food Devils launches on 3 November for PC, and you can download the free prologue demo on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: Water companies' environmental performance 'deteriorates' further - regulators
paragraphs: The environmental performance of water companies fell again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators into the industry.
Eight of the nine water companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.
Companies were praised for their continued provision of high-quality drinking water and reducing service disruptions.
But the chair of the environmental regulator said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".
