items.title: Ofcom sets out social media age-checking methods ahead of ban
paragraphs: Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.
A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.

Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.
To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:
photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check
banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age
face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)
digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age
The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.
However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.
Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:

"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.
"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."

Some of the tech companies, including Meta, have called for age verification to be applied at device level, so that someone under-age would be automatically blocked from installing social media apps via app stores.
This would place responsibility with Apple and Google, who between them operate most of the world's smartphones. Apple has already introduced age verification in the UK.
However Ofcom says that would not absolve the social network providers from doing their own checks as well.

The regulator said it didn't have a firm number for how many adults would need to prove they were not under age, but conceded that it would be a "large number of accounts" that social media companies would need to "deal with."
It has also acknowledged that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", and some children would succeed in bypassing the age checks.
Dawes said making the ban work would be a joint effort.
"At Ofcom, what we will do is make sure that the services that the social media companies put in the checks that they need to," she told BBC News.
"That's our job, but the wider question about how everybody engages with this, it is for everybody, really.

"I actually think the real prize here is going to be for today's eight to 10-year-olds entering secondary school without it being the norm to go on Snap in your class group chat, without it being the norm to have all your sports fixtures organised on Instagram."
Ofcom's age verification report will now be considered by the government, with a decision due by the end of the year.
Child safety campaigners including the Molly Rose Foundation and NSPCC welcomed Ofcom's guidance.
But both said there were lessons to be learned from how Australia's social media ban had been implemented, after it was found many under-16s could still access social platforms.

"That's why, as we prepare to embark on our own social media ban in the UK, we need to make sure we accurately know the age of child users," said Rani Govender, head of child safety online at the NSPCC.
She said the government and Ofcom must ensure tech firms are held accountable for meeting age check standards "to help keep children safe online and ensure the ban delivers change in practice".

But Andy Burrows, the Molly Rose Foundation's chief executive, said Ofcom had shown a "dire track record" of enforcing the Online Safety Act - raising questions over how effectively it would help deliver a social media ban.

"Andy Burnham must deliver a ban that learns the lessons from Australia and that incentivises safety-by-design as the price of admission to the UK market, with a ban as the starting point in a proper plan to give children a safe and happy online life," he said.
Jonny Blunt, corporate affairs director of BT's consumer division, said w families should "prepare children for life online after the ban and highlight the risks of trying to dodge the restrictions".
"Having those conversations now and giving young people time to prepare for the changes in March will be crucial in helping them adapt to a significant change for a whole generation," he said.

"The restrictions have the potential to change the way young people interact with the digital world for the better, but only if regulators, tech companies, families, and educators come together to make it a success."

items.title: Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea "without traditional thresholds"
paragraphs: Architecture studio Büro Ole Scheeren has revealed designs for the Suseong Continuum, a snaking, concrete art gallery in Daegu, South Korea.
Set to be built within the city’s Yeonhwaji park, the 364-square-metre gallery was designed specifically for showcasing digital art.
Berlin-based Büro Ole Scheeren designed the gallery as a continuous space, without any enclosed rooms and or doorways, in a bid to reflect the “flows” of digital art.
“We wanted to build a gallery without traditional thresholds: a gradient of realities that morph into one another as you gradually move through the space,” studio founder Ole Scheeren said.

“The substance of digital art is not rooted in the physical domain of distinct objects and isolated experiences… it exists in a world of overlaps and connections, where one condition potentially flows into the next.”
“Landscape, circulation and exhibition become a continuous experience,” the studio added.
The Suseong Continuum gallery was unveiled as part of this year’s Suseong International Biennale, which invites architects to realise permanent public works across Daegu.
Commissioned by the Suseong District Government, the design by Büro Ole Scheeren is expected to open for the biennale’s 2028 edition.
Once complete, visitors will access the space via a winding path, from which the gallery was designed to emerge as an extrusion.
Conceived as a “continuation of the landscape”, the gallery’s twisting volume will be partially embedded into the park’s topography and oriented toward a nearby lotus pond.
Its structure will be built using board-marked concrete to create a rough exterior texture. Inside, this textured surface will transition to smooth concrete walls for projecting media onto.
According to Büro Ole Scheeren, the gallery’s layout and materiality were designed to reflect the transition from the park’s natural landscape to the digital interiors.

“Technology is often seen as an opposite to nature,” Scheeren said. “With Suseong Continuum we wanted to explore how we can create a way of extending the way we perceive the relationship between both domains – a journey that starts in the park and that seamlessly carries you into the digital realm.”
“There is no single moment where one world ends and the other begins, it is a continuous transformation.”
“What begins as natural landscape gradually transforms into digital media,” the studio added.
Renders of the gallery’s stripped-back interior reveal its immersive exhibition spaces framed by curving walls.

A layered ceiling will run the building’s full length to conceal all lighting and technical infrastructure, which was developed by the studio in collaboration with the Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe.
“The interior unfolds as a spatial gradient in which light, sound, enclosure and immersion shift gradually along the visitor’s route,” the studio said.
“Curving walls widen into open spaces and tighten into passages; atmospheres transform rather than switch,” it added.
The design will remain on show at the Suseong International Biennale until 22 November.
In Shenzhen, China, the studio has revealed plans for skyscrapers with “waterfall” facades and its design for the Róng Museum of Arts is currently under construction.

items.title: Prada's hand-drawn holiday campaign is an utter joy – and a sharp lesson for Coca-Cola
paragraphs: As a kid, it's natural to love Christmas. As an adult, it's natural to get stressed out by it. But I have to admit, even when I reached middle age, I was still a sucker for that "Holidays are coming" chorus from the Coke ads that herald the arrival of the festive season.
Well, until a couple of years ago, anyhow.

For the last two Christmases, unfortunately, the soft drinks giant has ruined it all for me by sticking AI-generated effects into its commercials. Not just that, but actively boasting about it. (If you were lucky enough to miss last year's monstrosity, our article Coca-Cola's AI ad just ruined Christmas... again allows you to relive it in all its gruesome glory.)
Prada Holiday 2026 | "Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand" - YouTube

I mean, I can understand the shop down the road – the one that never seems to have any customers and is clearly operating on a shoestring – reaching for gen AI to save a few pennies. But a company valued at $400 billion? Do me a favour.

So it's a real pleasure to see Prada heading in the right direction here. Drawing Prada, its holiday campaign for 2026, brings its celeb ambassadors (Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke, Chen Haoyu, Kelvin Harrison Jr and Luther Ford) into cartoon worlds drawn entirely by hand.

A sardonic fox trails Maya through the snow; a goofy lynx peers out from behind a tree at Kelvin; and a trio of mice make off with Sadie's spotty loafers. It all feels very "classic Disney", and that's no coincidence.

The animation was directed by John Pomeroy, who started out at Disney in the 1970s, co-founded the studio behind The Secret of NIMH with Don Bluth, and later returned to the House of Mouse for Pocahontas.
Alongside him on the Prada campaign is lead animator Tom Bancroft, whose credits include Beauty and the Beast, Aladdin, The Lion King and Mulan.

"What's great is that John called the band back together," Tom explains in Prada's behind-the-scenes reel. "He called a bunch of us that had been working at other studios for many years doing traditional hand drawn animation. It's great to be back and doing this for Prada."
That experience and that enthusiasm show. Prada itself never mentions AI slop, but then it doesn't need to. This is the antidote, staring you in the face, and it's utterly delightful.

A campaign that puts experienced animators back to work, and celebrates what they do, is certainly something I'd like to see a lot more of. If a fashion house can see the value in that, then surely the world's biggest soft drinks brand can too. Over to you, Coca-Cola.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry
paragraphs: The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.
In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.

The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.
Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.

The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.
In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.

Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.
“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”
The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.

Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.
Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.
China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.
The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.

The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

items.title: Ever wondered what goes on inside a pair of earphones? These transparent IEMs reveal all
paragraphs: If you’re in the market for a pair of in-ear monitors (IEMs) that sound warm and smooth for under $200, here's a new option that's well worth checking out (though I advise you to look at our list of the best budget IEMs under $100).

I say this sensing that many people will be turned off by the brand's name, which is natural to read as "Awful". The fact, too, that its press release is set in the Comic Sans font means even some journalists might not take them seriously. But they should!

Marketing is one thing; technical achievement is another. And after getting a few days listening to these new earphones, what's important to me is that the MiracleOne, on sale today for $199.99, prioritises comfort and design just as much as sound quality. It's enough for me to consider it for our list of the best IEMs under $500.

What am I talking about? Well, the MiracleOne uses just one driver, so it’s tiny (6mm across, where most single-driver sets use 8-10mm). That means smaller shells, lessening the strain on your ears over long sessions. And the design is a really cool transparent resin that allows you to see what's going on inside. A design choice I can definitely get behind.

The shells are made from transparent resin, so you can see the gold 2-pin sockets, the acoustic tubing and a small black circuit board, finished off with a polished metal nozzle. In short, if you like seeing the gubbins in your gear – the sort of approach popularised by the Nothing range – you’ll love it. If you don't, you won't.

The driver is made from a soft, springy silicone material, and sits inside two small sound chambers designed to tune the sound. One of these is designed to take the harsh edge off high notes. The other keeps the bass tight.

Handily, the cable detaches from the earpieces, so you can replace it if it breaks. You also get a carrying case and ear tips in three styles, each of which tweaks the sound slightly (fuller, clearer or more spacious). Note that you’ll need to pick your plug when you order. The standard 3.5mm suits most people, while the 4.4mm might be better for dedicated music players and headphone amps.

Here's the killer question, though: how does it compare with similarly priced IEMs? Well, listening to the MiracleOne, I immediately thought of the classic New Meta Kiwi Ears KE4 – one of our choices among the best IEMs under $500?

The KE4 is a hybrid with two dynamic drivers and two balanced armatures, while the MiracleOne relies on just one driver. Both have a warm, easy-going sound, but the KE4’s big strength is its midrange – vocals and instruments come through rich and detailed, backed by a wad of bass that can sometimes get a bit boomy.

I'd say that both the KE4 and the MiracleOne share a similar deep, rumbling bass, but MiracleOne has better separation between that bass and the midrange. They're both smooth in the upper mids, but I feel that vocals are a little more forward with MO than the KE4.

Ultimately, I think this is a strong single-dynamic IEM that trades punches with an established classic, so it's well worth checking out. The fact that it looks better than 90% of IEMs isn't going to hurt its chances of success either.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
paragraphs: Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".

Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."

When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".

items.title: Actor targets 'scarred villain' screen stereotype
paragraphs: An actor is backing a charity's call for more positive roles for performers with scars and visible differences.

Northamptonshire-based Robert Rhodes, who has appeared in Silent Witness and House of the Dragon, said: "The media industry needs to start reflecting the true experience of people with visible difference."

The charity Changing Faces wants the film and TV industry to stop using scars, burns and other visible differences as marks of villainy and has started a petition calling for more positive representation.
One casting agency said visible differences were often used as a shorthand for villainy, but that these casting briefs could be successfully challenged.

New research by the Centre for Appearance Research (CAR) at the University of the West of England showed that people who are exposed to visible difference via villainous characters go on to have a more negative perception of people with visible difference in the real world, the charity said.

Rhodes, who was recently in the BBC One show, The Rapture, was born with a large facial birthmark as a result of congenital melanocytic nevus and was left with scarring following multiple surgeries to remove it as a child.
He said: "We can't wait for action any longer.
"Yes, there is often trauma associated with a scar, but we experience joy, love and success just like everyone else.
"More neutral and aspirational characters on screen will improve real perceptions of the whole visible difference community."
Fellow actor Beau Bradfield said: "As an actor with facial scarring, I know how important it is to see people with visible differences represented on screen as real, complex people.
"I want children growing up with visible differences to see characters who look like them being heroes, friends, parents and love interests – not just villains."
About 4.9 million people in the UK have a visible difference, the charity said.

As part of its work to monitor visible difference representation, it has worked with the Creative Diversity Network to include visible difference as a category in its diversity data monitoring and reporting.
Louise Wright, chief executive of Changing Faces, said: "For years we've asked the industry to think about the stories it tells about visible difference.
"Now, for the first time, we have proof that those stories don't stay on screen – they shape how people with visible difference are treated in real life.
"Halloween is the moment this is impossible to ignore, which is why we're asking industry, and the public, to help us change it."
Bailey Frances, from Cambridge-based Shakyra Dowling Casting, a member of the Casting Directors' Association, said: "Getting it right matters.

"Villains are often written with visible differences (eg facial scars) as shorthand, but asking whether a character could be interpreted differently, or whether that difference is essential to the story, leads to better, more truthful storytelling," she said.
"We regularly present actors who don't match the description on the page but fit the character perfectly, and they're often the ones who get the job.
"Casting directors are in a unique position to widen the search and open up the conversation with writers and directors, challenging the initial casting briefs where needed."

items.title: RAF base chemical contamination worst in UK, report says
paragraphs: Chemical contamination at a former RAF base earmarked for 9,000 homes is the worst found in the UK, a report has said.
Testing at RAF Upper Heyford carried out on behalf of a developer found "unacceptable" levels of polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), referred to as forever chemicals.
Fears have been raised previously that the site could be the source of pollution in nearby waterways, after earlier testing by campaigners and the Environment Agency.
Paul Silver, chief executive of developer Dorchester Living, said separate soil samples taken from residential areas showed the area was "safe for use".
PFAS are a group of thousands of man-made chemicals, some of which can cause cancer, which are often referred to as forever chemicals because they do not break down easily.
The results of the site investigations were uploaded to Cherwell District Council's website as part of a planning application.
The author of the report said they were higher than the village of Bentham, Yorkshire, "determined as having the highest level of PFAS in the UK".
The Environment Agency (EA) said military sites and airports were hotspots for PFAS, which were used extensively in firefighting foams for decades.
At RAF Upper Heyford, firefighters would practice putting out an aeroplane set on fire above a "pond" of fuel.
This training area was found to be "the most significant ongoing source of PFAS contamination identified".
Another report into ground and surface water found contamination was "widespread" at the site, with all samples exceeding environmental standards.
Subsequent independent testing by Gallos Brook Environmental Group found elevated levels of the chemicals in more than a dozen streams that flow from beneath the base.
The results have prompted concerns from residents about existing and approved developments near the site, including a primary school.
Groundwater and surface water results from the school site in another report showed PFAS exceeded safe levels by environmental quality standards.
Calum Miller, MP for Bicester and Woodstock, said: "The most important thing is to understand fully what level of contamination, if any, there is in that area.
"And in the case of a primary school that people have real confidence that it's a safe environment for children."
The BBC has spoken to residents living near the site who would like their blood tested to determine if they have been disproportionately exposed.
One of them, Leigh Radwell, said she was concerned for her health after eating vegetables from her garden.
She said: "My little countryside haven and my dream of growing my own veg and having chickens and supporting wildlife is ruined.
Helen Christie, from Gallos Brook Environmental Group, said the results confirmed what campaigners had been saying: "That the site is contaminated."
But she said the testing done so far had been "inadequate".
"The duty of care now must be towards the 1,300 houses already built and those living in the surrounding areas," she added.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea – level 1
paragraphs: The UK government says yes to getting new gas from under the sea. There is a plan to drill in the North Sea.
Leaders say that this gas will help keep the country safe when energy prices are high. The prime minister says that the country still needs gas, but it also wants clean energy in the future.

Many people are very angry about this decision. They say that getting more gas is bad for the planet. It will not help people get cheaper electricity. They want the government to use clean power like wind and sun instead of oil and gas.
Difficult words: drill (to make a hole in the earth to get oil or gas), price (how much money something costs), decision (what you do after thinking or talking about it).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea – level 2
paragraphs: The UK government approved a new project to drill for gas in the North Sea. Energy companies say this project will help produce more gas for the country.

Leaders argue that using local gas makes the country safer as global conflict causes energy prices to rise. The prime minister explained that the country still needs gas while moving toward green energy.

Environmental groups and green politicians strongly disagree with the plan. They warn that drilling produces harmful emissions and will not lower electricity bills for normal families. Activists argue that the government should focus on renewable energy like wind and solar instead of fossil fuels.
Difficult words: approve (to officially agree), harmful (when something hurts living things or the planet), renewable energy (energy from natural sources, such as wind, sun, and so on).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea – level 3
paragraphs: The British government has approved drilling at a controversial North Sea gas field, despite strong opposition from environmental groups.

Energy companies welcomed the decision and predicted the project could supply over six percent of the nation’s gas at peak production. Officials argue that developing domestic resources is necessary to boost national energy security while global conflicts drive up fuel costs. The prime minister stated that although the country remains committed to long-term climate targets, oil and gas will still be needed during the transition to renewable energy.

However, climate activists and politicians heavily criticized the approval and warned that increased fossil fuel reliance won’t lower household energy bills because prices are dictated by international markets. They stress that true security requires a faster shift toward clean energy rather than expanding fossil fuel infrastructure.

Difficult words: controversial (causing a lot of angry public discussion and strong disagreement), dictate (to state, order, or control authoritatively how something must be done or decide), reliance (dependence on someone or something for help or support).
