items.title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
paragraphs: Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.
The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.

“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.

Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.

“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.

“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.
Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.

The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.

Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.
The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.

“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.
Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.

With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.

In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.

“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.

Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.
Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.
The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

items.title: Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
paragraphs: Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital.

Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings.

Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather.

The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition, and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing.

The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces.

Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture.
“Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen.
“We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.”

Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine.
“The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said.

The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom, who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project, the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas.
Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future.

For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space.

In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold.

The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions.
Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut.
Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving.
Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

items.title: The rise and fall of mid-century modern: how millennials fell out of love with their favourite look
paragraphs: “I definitely don’t think it is cringe,” says Laura Budds, a vintage furniture dealer based in Norfolk. “But I do think we have reached the peak, and we’re on the descent.” Budds is talking about mid-century modern furniture, which has recently come under fire from younger generations for being – like so many things, including trainer socks and high-waisted jeans – a deeply millennial aesthetic. As the Wall Street Journal declared: “Midcentury modern design has met the fate of pumpkin spice lattes, cocktails in mason jars, no-show socks, leggings and other aspects of millennial culture: it has become cringey.”

Budds, 44, is resigned to the fact that she is a “mid-century millennial”. She’s even made a career out of it: she sells furniture and vintage clothes at Williams & Parfitt, a modern antiques centre in Wymondham, Norfolk. But she says she has had to diversify in recent years to cater to changing tastes among younger customers, who are moving away from the “wall-to-wall mid-century” look beloved by the generation above them. She says of gen Z: “I don’t think they are so bound by the eras or designers – they just buy what they like. They aren’t afraid of older antiques and will have a bit of whimsy or taxidermy.”

The term “mid-century modern” was originally coined to refer to architecture and design that became popular from the 1940s to the 1970s, largely in the US, Brazil and Europe. Famed for its clean lines and simplicity, the style had visual forebears in the Bauhaus movement and classic Scandinavian design, along with the philosophy of beautiful yet functional furniture for the masses that spread to the US, UK and beyond in the postwar era. British-made items include Ercol and Robin Day chairs and G Plan teak sideboards, all of which are still coveted. (Anglepoise’s timeless industrial lighting, too, was associated with the aesthetic.)

The book Mid-Century Modern: Furniture of the 1950s, written by Cara Greenberg and published in 1984, is often seen as being responsible for popularising the phrase. Today, she says, the term has “become meaningless, applied to everything from museum-quality material to made-in-China repros on eBay”.

Greenberg lives in Brooklyn, New York. Her first mid-century purchase was an Eames plywood lounge chair bought at a street market in NYC in the 1970s, which she still owns. These days, she is more interested in a comfy sofa: “not a mid-century modern speciality”, she says, given the aesthetic’s tendency for furniture to be fairly upright and firm, often designed with polite conversation in mind rather than slouching and scrolling.

But, Greenberg says, she will still defend the best of it “as the most innovative and stylish furniture America ever came up with”: Charles and Ray Eames, the husband and wife duo who revolutionised design with multipurpose chairs; George Nelson’s industrial looks for the furniture company Herman Miller; Eero Saarinen’s Tulip chair for Knoll. Since then, she says, “there have been many cycles of revival, including the reissue and mass marketing of ‘best of’ classics by the original companies in the 1990s”.

Affordability has always been a cornerstone of mid-century design. “The philosophy of modernism and mid-century design, when it first started, was accessibility,” says Keith Stephenson, who lives in Camberwell, south-east London with his partner, Mark Hampshire. Together they run the design and homewares company Mini Moderns and co-authored the 2019 book Mid-Century Modern Living: The Mini Moderns Guide to Pattern and Style. “It was never supposed to be an elitist thing,” he says. “It was about bringing good design at a good price to as many people as possible. Reaching more people with good design is never a bad thing.”

It is also ideal for smaller spaces, which is one of the reasons Hampshire thinks it has “endured many a cycle of trends” to become “the endlessly go-to period of design”. The postwar period was “the first time that designers considered function and aesthetics together – so furniture was designed to solve a specific problem as well as to fulfil a function. The results of this level of considered design have, in many cases, proved hard to beat, thus becoming the template for subsequent designs.”

He gives an example: “If you look at a classic mid-century style sofa, it is on legs, so you can see the floor underneath it – and that makes a place feel much bigger, because you can read the room around the piece of furniture. There’s room to breathe. All of those things are classic interior design tricks to make a place look and feel more spacious.”

Mid-century modern’s design quality and price point made it irresistible to millennials who were starting to live independently in the 2010s. It fitted with the vintage aesthetic of the time and there were still bargains to be found. Even as late as 2019, says Budd, “you could find sideboards at auction for £50. Now you’re lucky to get one for less than £300-£400.” A lot of British mid-century modern has been shipped abroad in recent years, to Europe and as far as Japan, where consumers have cottoned on to British brands such as Ercol, G Plan and McIntosh. This has pushed prices up and “made it a bit too elitist. Only certain people can afford the really good quality stuff now,” says Budd.

The interior designer Natasha Landers has lived in her home in Walthamstow, east London, for 26 years. Her mid-century bookcase cost £30 when she bought it, and her £50 coffee table would now sell for £200. “It’s not as accessible as it was when I first started collecting,” she says. Still, she’s reluctant to write off the whole aesthetic just because it has been widely used. “Good design doesn’t have to become bad design because it is popular,” says Landers. “There is something slightly snobbish about deciding something is no longer cool simply because more people can enjoy it. What I do have a problem with is when everyone’s houses look the same.”

The proliferation of millennial style on the go-to interior design sources Pinterest and Instagram has inevitably meant that the high street and large webstores have capitalised on the trend. New furniture clearly inspired by classic mid-century modern pieces can now be found everywhere from Marks & Spencer and Dunelm to H&M and Temu.

“That craze for buying a full set of mid-century tables, sofas and lighting is definitely gone,” says Carina Harford, an interior designer from west London. “It had a paint-by-numbers experience to it that might have felt safe to its devotees but began to feel too commonplace.” The climate impact of “fast furniture” is also a consideration. “The imitation mid-century furniture that was coming out a lot in the last five or so years really irked me,” says Harford. “Stop buying new things if you don’t need them.”

It is this desire to avoid having identikit homes that is fuelling the mid-century modern cringe. “I really don’t want to have the same things as everyone else,” says Sheree Millington, a copywriter based in Margate, who is renovating her Victorian terrace. Lucy Hayes, a writer and director in east London, agrees. “I like a mix of styles and ages, and things that don’t feel rooted to a particular decade or era. I want my home to feel like it exists now rather than as a time capsule.”

Millington thinks a more quintessentially English style is coming back in, “whether that is cottagecore, or more like an English townhouse, with lots of mismatched things, more pattern, more print”. She is noticing chrome – a staple of 1990s homeware that has since fallen out of favour – becoming more popular again, too.

Harford’s home is kitted out with secondhand treasures spanning many different eras and styles: “It’s all just sort of mushed together, and I think it works.” Most of it was bought from auctions and cost about £100 or less. Highlights include a Victorian fold-out card table (bought for £110), lighting from a shuttered billiards hall (£40), a 1940s Anglo-Indian table (£30) and a set of 1980s stools (£90 for four). Although bidding can seem more complicated than buying new online for next day delivery, you quickly get the hang of it, she says, and the result is, “something much more special and unique”.

items.title: C Next Designers EMEA brings together over 250 professionals for design conference in Almería
paragraphs: For the ninth edition of the C Next Designers design conference, Spanish brand Cosentino brought together designers from Europe, Africa and the Middle East for three days of talks focused on “design as a driver of change”.
The event was held from 13 to 16 October in venues across Almería, Spain and included talks by designers such as Ron Arad, Karim Rashid and design studio Studiopepe.
It is the fourth iteration of the event held in Spain and the ninth worldwide.
This year’s conference focused on the theme Design to Transform, which champions “design as a force capable of reshaping society and adding value to it”, according to the team.
The first day opened with a welcome at the Cabo Gata Beach Hotel.
On Wednesday, the event moved to Cosentino’s industrial park in Cantoria, where Cosentino CEO Pilar Cosentino gave opening remarks.

Architect and designer Ron Arad then spoke with Cosentino commercial director for Europe, Jorge Lope about his career and collaborations with the brand, before the day ended with a guided tour of Cosentino’s facilities, including a local natural stone warehouse.
The day also featured the presentation of the latest product innovations by Valentín Tijeras, global vice president of product.
The second day took place at the Almería Science and Technology Park (PITA) and included presentations by brands Novara, Jung, Speho, TECE and Gaggenau.
Karim Rashid and Studiopepe then gave keynote speeches, which were a highlight of the day.
Dezeen editorial director (special projects) Max Fraser also moderated two panels as part of the event.

The first, held with Dornbracht, focused on hyper-personalisation as a creative tool and featured C’est Ici Design founder Monica Arango, founder of Black Architecture Danko Lekic and head of global channel management at Dornbracht Sascha Bialoian.

The second panel examined how design is changing our everyday habits, and featured Fran Silvestre Arquitectos founder Fran Silvestre, ZHA associate director Bidisha Sinha and founder of AS Architect Ayşin Sevgi Karakurt Macit.
Studio Haus closed the panels, and the event concluded with a gala dinner in the Cloister of Almería Cathedral, which was informed by the Dekton Artik Nodes collection, a new Cosentino material.
Cosentino previously launched Nara, a beige-toned porcelain surface designed to celebrate natural stone and Éclos, which was designed to be free of crystalline silica.
Last year’s C Next Designers conference featured talks by Sabine Marcelis and Peter Ippolito or Nini Andrade Silva.
To learn more about C Next Designers, visit the conference’s website.

items.title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
paragraphs: Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.

The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.

They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.

Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”
They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”
The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment.
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.

The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

items.title: 'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
paragraphs: Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.

Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.

Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.

In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.

"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".

The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.

Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".

Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.

It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

items.title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
paragraphs: Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.
On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).
Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.
Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.
The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.
Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres.
Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.
Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.
The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.
The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."

items.title: Stars and scars: the art of Atong Atem at the NGV – in pictures
paragraphs: The National Gallery of Victoria presents the first major Australian solo exhibition of the Melbourne artist, whose work references African studio photography, family archives, Catholic imagery and science fiction, while paying tribute to the myths and traditions of Dinka Bor culture in South Sudan. Passage: The Art of Atong Atem will run from Friday until 14 June at the Ian Potter Centre in Federation Square. Entry is free Keeping it real: the vivid photography of Atong Atem – in pictures Continue reading...

items.title: Family row over George Michael items up for auction - including Faith guitar
paragraphs: A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.
The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.
Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.
Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.
Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.
Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.
There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.
Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.

In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".
He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".
Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.
Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.
She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.
"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.
"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."
The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.
The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.
Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".
It has an estimated price tag of between £60,000 and £120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.
A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to £600 and a current bid of £1,750.

Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.
The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music.
"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.
He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart".
"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.
Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".
He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".
Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

items.title: Investors turn on Google owner Alphabet after profit miss, ad slowdown and high spending
paragraphs: Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell more than 10% in after-hours trading Wednesday, erasing tens of billions of dollars in stock market value from the $4tn tech giant. The company had reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.
Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn in the July-to-September period, or $2.12 a share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.
Alphabet booked an $8.7bn loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.
Revenue, however, rose 25% to an enormous $127.6bn. The figure was slightly below the roughly $128bn analysts had forecast.

Advertising revenue grew 11% to $82bn, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12% to $63.4bn, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.

YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to $11.2bn, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.
Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to $30.7bn, ahead of analyst expectations.
The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to $11.1bn.
Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy some of the chips.
Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of $372m and an operating loss of $2bn.
Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach 1m weekly rides by the end of the year.
Alphabet spent $51.4bn on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on datacenters and AI chips, more than double the $24bn a year earlier.
Its latest forecast for capex spending is between $195bn to $205bn in spending for 2026.
The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.
“I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise,” Sundar Pichai, the Google CEO, told analysts of the company’s investment splurge.
The company’s spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet’s businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a $9.1bn gap.
During the quarter Alphabet raised $28.7bn by selling bonds and $12.4bn by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.
Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.
It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.
The Gemini app has reached 1bn users. Google’s AI models now process nearly 32bn tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google’s largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.
In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.

items.title: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
paragraphs: Construction of tourism and housing facilities has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand
Environmental correspondent, BBC World Service
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.
Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.

In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.
The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.

The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.
The major tourist hub of Pokhara has seen major development in recent years
Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.
They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.
It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.

Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.
"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."
To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides.

Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."

Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."

Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.
The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".
"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."
Moment buildings are swept away as flash flood hits Nepal's Budhi Gandaki river
But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants.

"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.
And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.
The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.

But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.
Two months after the devastating August floods, these buildings in Trishuli Bazar remain devastated

The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.
This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.
The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.
Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.
"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."

Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.
But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.

Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.
Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.
"A fragile ecosystem like the Himalaya demands stricter planning and building regulations than elsewhere, yet these rules have been weak and poorly enforced."

Authorities in Nepal say they are working to address these issues. Settlements within 15m (49ft) of the riverbank along the recently devastated Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi corridor will soon be banned, according to the national disaster agency. Similar rules are being introduced in other river corridors soon.
"It is a challenging job because people in many places have sentimental attachments with their land and property but we cannot ignore the increasing risks," says chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety.
There has been "rampant construction" in the Indian state of Uttarakhand in areas at risk from flooding, activists say

A similar story has unfolded across Nepal's western border in India's Uttarakhand state, where maximum tourism limits and environmental regulations have been bypassed in the name of economic growth, claims activist Anoop Nautiyal.
On paper there are zoning rules prohibiting the construction of houses and infrastructure too close to river banks, "but on the ground we see no implementation of such rules.
"You can see rampant construction all over."

The Uttarakhand government on 12 October approved new floodplain zoning rules to regulate land use and development. "Its objective is to protect life, property and important infrastructure from possible flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of flood waters," the state's cabinet decision read.
But Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribuvan University, thinks it will not be possible to mitigate such threats completely.

Insurance grades, he suggests, could be another way to encourage people to build in less risky areas. If authorities were to map places as high, moderate and low risk, he believes insurance coverage would "follow accordingly" ensuring people who build homes in safer areas get better protection.
But for now, the pace of construction across the region shows no signs of slowing.

items.title: Microsoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees
paragraphs: Microsoft gained billions of dollars in stock market value Wednesday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, just days after it offered voluntary buyouts to some 60,000 employees.
The office software giant’s growth was fueled by its Azure cloud computing division, which grew by 48% in the September quarter.
“We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost-efficiency for customers across our entire stack,” Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said in a statement.

The technology giant recorded $92.3bn in total revenue and more than $36.6bn in profit, the company said in a securities filing Wednesday. Analysts had expected around $90.6bn in revenue and $35.1bn in profit, according to FactSet.

The quarterly earnings report comes two days after Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence investments.
It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year, after giving seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early in April.
Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.

Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than $2,500. Apple announced a similar touchscreen Macbook this week.

The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud datacenters, where running AI is slower and more expensive.

items.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
paragraphs: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses, and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work that they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted in leaks or hacks.
A representative of the DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was put online on Wednesday by a group called the Department of Peace alongside cybersecurity researcher and hacker maia crimew.
The information was put in a database named Icepick and shared through a website hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the goal of the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
The Department of Peace said on Wednesday that it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked with a group called ShinyHunters taking personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

items.title: Mbappé, Real Madrid forced to apologize over 'dictator' comment about China's Mao Zedong
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
France and Real Madrid soccer star Kylian Mbappé is facing a backlash in China after commercial sponsors cut ties with him over comments he made about China's founding leader Mao Zedong.
In a recent interview Mbappé described finding a meme—which photoshopped him onto an image resembling that of Mao and referred to it as a "Chinese dictator."
Mbappé has since issued a public apology for his comments as Chinese brands dropped Mbappe and a broadcaster suspended broadcasting Spain's La Liga matches.

In an apology issued on Tuesday in both Chinese and French, Mbappé said that his comment during a recent interview was “ill-judged”, adding that he now understands that it hurt "many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world."
A U.S. congressional committee on China said Mbappé should not have apologized for calling Mao Zedong a "dictator."

The U.S. House Select Committee on China posted a statement on X, saying that Mao Zedong "was indeed a dictator, and the harm he inflicted upon the Chinese people was far more severe than anything a soccer player might say."

The committee, chaired by Congressman John Moolenaar (R-MI), followed up with a repost of a video it recently created about the Cultural Revolution, which Mao launched 60 years ago, calling it “one of the darkest chapters in Chinese history”.
Former Turkish American basketball player and rights activist Enes Kanter Freedom also suggested he disagreed with Mbappe's apology.

“I'm not here to judge Mbappe for apologizing. I don't know what pressure he faced,” Freedom told VOA Tuesday. “But you know, when athletes feel they have to choose between their principles and their careers, we have a serious problem. So that's why I think it's a shame that he came out and apologized because Mao Zedong is a dictator.”

A video clip from an interview with Mbappé on the French show The Bridge has been circulating on social media platforms since Monday. When asked which meme featuring his likeness is the funniest, Mbappé mentioned one where his face is superimposed onto an image of a "Chinese dictator."

Mbappé did not name the character by name, but the show’s post-production team inserted an image of his face superimposed onto a portrait of Mao, implying that he was referring to Mao, triggering the backlash in China.

The following day, several Chinese enterprises—including beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu, and cheese maker Milkground, moved to terminate all partnerships with Mbappé, saying they had "zero-tolerance" policy toward "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people". The official China Central Television (CCTV) began suspending all broadcasts related to the Spanish football league LALIGA and matches involving Mbappé, and all advertisements featuring him have been pulled.

Mbappé, the 2026 World Cup Golden Boot winner currently plays for Real Madrid in Spain. He helped France win the 2018 World Cup and scored a hattrick in the 2022 World Cup final. Mbappé is considered one of the most influential and commercially valuable soccer players in the world today. Until this week's incident, he had multiple lucrative sponsorship deals with Chinese companies.
Spain's premier league football known as La Liga has issued an official apology to China over Mbappé’s comment on Tuesday. Real Madrid issued a similar apology Wednesday.
Asked about Mbappe's apology during a regular press briefing in Beijing Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "We take seriously the apology that the person has made."

Mao Zedong who led China from 1949 until his death in 1976 is revered in China as the “Great Leader” and the main founder of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People’s Republic China. In the 1980’s, Chinese authorities, in their attempt to launch reforms and break away from the Cultural Revolution era, once acknowledged some “serious mistakes” made by Mao. However, the current leader Xi Jinping has publicly expressed his admiration for Mao and called him a "great patriot and national hero of China in modern times."

Mao’s critics in China and abroad view him as one of the deadliest dictators in human history. In its X post, the U.S. House Select Committee on China alleged that Mao's "dictatorship and disastrous policies killed tens of millions of Chinese people in the Cultural Revolution, the Great Famine, and other atrocities.”

The committee’s post added: “The real disgrace in this news story is the companies rushing to apologize so they can continue to do business in China. The CCP is the largest oppressor of the Chinese people and their human rights, and those businesses that work with the CCP help normalize its crushing brutality.”
Mbappé is not the first sports figure to face varying degrees of censorship or boycotts in China due to their public comments.

Ironically, it was a former Real Madrid and Arsenal star, Mesut Özil who, through social media post, criticized Chinese government policies and the detention of Uyghurs in Xinjiang in December 2019. Özil left Arsenal in 2021 to joint Turkish club Fenerbahçe though it's unclear whether it was related to the comments he made about China.

Freedom himself faced similar problems when he criticized Chinse communist party in October 2021. After making remarks on social media and during games that were critical of Chinese actions in Tibet, Xinjiang, and Taiwan, broadcasts of games featuring his then-team, the Boston Celtics, were halted in China. Chinse platforms such as Tencent Sports also scrubbed all videos and merchandise related to him.

Chinese companies also suspended broadcasting NBA games after two NBA-related incidents involving the former General Manager of the NBA’s Houston Rockets, Daryl Morey, and former LA Lakers star Dwight Howard in 2019 and in 2023. The suspensions cost the NBA millions of dollars in revenue from broadcasting rights.
VOA Mandarin’s Stella Hsu contributed to this article.

items.title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
paragraphs: The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.

A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.

The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.

Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.

At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.

Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.

Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.

items.title: Former Russian detainee’s sister says Stephen Hubbard ‘escaped hell’
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

The sister of former Russian detainee Stephen Hubbard says her brother's condition is better than the family expected. The 74-year-old American was released from Russia after more than four years in detention and returned to the United States last week.

"It was incredible. I don’t even know how to describe it. It’s simply unbelievable to realize that he is free and has escaped the hell he spent nearly five years in," his sister, Patricia Hubbard, said in a recent interview with VOA.
"He underwent all the examinations and tests. Now he needs to rebuild his muscles and regain his strength," she said.

Russian forces detained Stephen Hubbard in the Russian occupied-Ukrainian town of Izium in April of 2022, where he had lived and taught English since 2014. Russia convicted him of being a mercenary and sentenced him to six to 10 years in a penal colony in October of 2024. Patricia Hubbard says her brother was never a mercenary.
"That was just a pretext to take his property," she told VOA, adding that her brother had absolutely no intention of joining the Ukrainian military or taking part in the Russia-Ukraine war.

"He hated the war. He was against it. Stephen was never a military man. Yes, he served in the U.S. Air Force, but that was not during wartime," she said. "As a child, he never got into fights. He wasn’t one of those boys who was always getting into trouble. He was a good, quiet child who took part in the [Boy] Scouts and read a great deal. He always loved books."
Patricia Hubbard told VOA that she heard of her brother's possible release about two days before it happened.

"I was told that everything could change at the last minute," she said. "They [U.S. officials] did say, expect anything to happen at the last minute because that's happened before when a country will say they're going to let someone out, then they like to torture you by not letting them out [until the] last minute."
She noted that the moment she saw her brother was special.
"We just hugged. We kept telling each other, “I love you,” over and over again. We hugged for a long time," Patricia Hubbard said.

Stephen Hubbard spent the first days in the U.S. under medical evaluation. His sister says after a medical assessment, he was sent home with a new set of clothes, new medical records, a new passport, and identification.
"When someone is taken hostage, they lose everything. Everything is stripped from them," she told VOA.
Patricia, who holds a master's in psychological counseling, said she chose not to talk to her brother about his experience in the Russian jail, where she said he was tortured.
"Some of the guards who knew only a few words in English would shout, 'Die, American, die!' while beating him," she said.

"Psychologically, he is doing much better than expected," Hubbard said. "His faith has helped him enormously. Psychologically, he has been through a great deal. But he did say one thing. He said, 'I want to be around people I know and who love me.' He said there is no love in that place. No love at all. Only darkness."
While in the Russian jail, Patricia says her brother Stephen spent most of his time in complete isolation.

"And even when someone else was nearby, they didn’t speak the same language," she told VOA. "There was no television or radio. He had no sense of time. He had absolutely no idea how much the world had changed over the past five years. All of it is a shock to him. It’s as if you had fallen into a coma and then woken up.”

items.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
paragraphs: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.
The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.
Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.
"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.
Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

items.title: Liverpool's Littlewoods film studios plan given £20m Budget boost
paragraphs: An artist's impression of how the Littlewoods building could look after its redevelopment into a film and television production campus
The government has pledged £20m towards plans to transform Liverpool's derelict Littlewoods building into a film and television production campus.
The funding, announced in the Budget earlier, will come from the government's Growth Mission Fund but is subject to final business case approval.

The long-delayed project would see the former Littlewoods Pools headquarters on Edge Lane turned into a 260,000 sq ft (six-acre, 2.4-hectare) creative campus for film, television, gaming and other digital screen industries.
It is unclear whether the money will be enough to meet the project's funding needs - Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram previously sought £50m in government support.
Steve Rotheram previously sought £50m government investment
Plans to turn the landmark Art Deco building into a film and television complex have been discussed since 2017 but have faced repeated delays.
In February, Rotheram said he was "desperate" to get the project "off the ground", but acknowledged a funding gap.
At the time, the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority had committed up to £17m towards the scheme.
Developer Capital & Centric had previously warned that the cost of delivering the project "in the current climate exceeds the value of the completed development".
Liverpool City Council said the new investment would support the wider redevelopment of the site, known as the Liverpool Creative Campus.
BBC crime drama This City is Ours is among the productions filmed in Liverpool
Deputy council leader Ruth Bennett welcomed the announcement by Chancellor John Healey.
"It is one of Liverpool's great landmarks and its redevelopment presents an enormous opportunity to build on our success as one of the UK's leading locations for film and television," she said.
However, Liverpool councillor Kris Brown, who said he had raised concerns about the project's financial risks in 2021, called for strict oversight of the new funding.
"While this funding is a massive step forward, the hard work starts now," he said. "We cannot afford any more false dawns.
"The developers must urgently get a main contractor on site, and the council must implement rigorous, transparent oversight."
Brown also called for guarantees that the promised jobs, training opportunities and studio facilities would be delivered.
Built in 1938, the Littlewoods building was once used to process football pools betting slips, in which people tried to predict the results of matches.
The building closed in 1994 and was badly damaged by a fire in 2018, adding to delays in its redevelopment.
Work to clear and make the site safe began in December 2023, and planning permission for construction was granted in October 2024.
The Growth Mission Fund was set up to invest £240m between 2026-27 and 2029-30 in schemes designed to boost job creation and the economic regeneration of local communities.
The Budget also announced additional national funding for affordable housing and tackling homelessness, which Liverpool City Council said could support its work in the city.
