Photography by Jason O'Rear (unless otherwise stated)

items.title: ‘Light therapy without remortgaging the house’: the best LED face masks – tested
paragraphs: LED face masks are booming in popularity – despite being one of the most expensive at-home beauty products to hit the market. They claim to reduce the appearance of fine lines, stop spots and calm redness, with some even combining different types of light to enhance the benefits.

However, it’s wise to be sceptical about new treatments that are costly and non-invasive, and to do your research before you buy. With this in mind, I interviewed doctors and dermatologists to find out whether these light therapy devices work.

They’re not a miracle cure for deep-set wrinkles, but experts say the best light therapy masks can promote collagen production, improve elasticity and help smooth skin with sustained use. And while it may seem like a new technology, research from the 1990s shows the efficacy of light therapy in wound healing, acne treatment and skin rejuvenation.
Red and infrared light are safe to use on all skin types, but be warned that blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones.
I’ve tested some of the most popular devices on the market – including infrared masks – to narrow down my favourite LED face masks for treating a range of skin concerns.
Best LED mask overallCurrentBody Series 3
Best budget LED face maskSilk’n LED face mask 100
Best LED mask for full facial coverageTherabody TheraFace mask Glo
Best LED device for acne-prone skinLustre Solo
Best LED mask for quick treatmentsDr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWare Pro
Best LED mask for travelSilk’n LED face mask Pro

I’ve been reviewing health and beauty tech for the past five years. During this time I’ve witnessed many beauty fads come and go. Naturally tight-fisted and a sceptic, I was initially struck by the cost of these masks. How on earth can an elaborate LED light strip set you back more than £300?

But after testing multiple light therapy masks, I’ve come to understand the technology behind them – and, sadly, you won’t be able to engineer your own light therapy system with a costume mask and a set of LED string lights.

I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles to test on, but I can comment on how blue-light treatment affects acne because I’ve suffered from it since I was a teenager – despite my mum’s assurances that it would clear up after puberty. The experts I spoke to agreed on the efficacy of red and infrared light for anti-ageing.

Light therapy masks are fantastic additions to a skincare routine, helping to smooth, firm and reduce blemishes. Since I started using one almost two years ago, my skin is calmer, less prone to redness, and has a more even tone.

However, LED masks can be expensive, and if you’re not disciplined enough to use one regularly, you won’t see results. Before you splash up to £500, keep in mind that light therapy masks are most effective when paired with a good skincare routine. It’s crucial to make sure skin is properly cleansed before treatment and protected from sun damage afterwards.

If you don’t already have a skincare routine nailed down, don’t buy a light therapy mask just yet. Consider starting out using a gentle cleanser and moisturiser, with an SPF for daytime. You could also incorporate targeted skincare serums, such as retinol and vitamin C, to help firm and brighten the skin without the need for an expensive light therapy mask.

Since LED treatments take a while to show visible results, it’s difficult to test multiple light therapy masks at once (at least, without spending a few years testing them), so I enlisted the help of dermatologists who were familiar with light therapy treatments long before they were commercially available.

I spoke to Dr Barbara Kubicka, an expert in aesthetic medicine; Dr Derrick Phillips, a consultant dermatologist and spokesperson for the British Skin Foundation; and aesthetic doctor Dr Priya Verma, an authority on the science of skin ageing.

I asked these experts to identify which light therapy mask features – such as bulb quality and quantity, light wavelength and treatment time – matter the most, to inform my choices. They also outlined the suitability of light therapy for different skin types and its associated risks.

Armed with their advice, I tested the fit, comfort levels and usability of 18 of the most popular light therapy masks and other targeted LED devices. Getting hands on with the masks allowed me to pinpoint any of the key features the experts recommended, as well as features I found helpful as a consumer.

I’ve been using a light therapy mask regularly for almost two years, so I can identify a good mask from a bad one. My tests also included monitoring results after four nightly sessions, with the obvious caveat that only very minimal changes could be observed after such a short-term treatment. I then tested my favourite masks over several months, too, helping me to verify any unique treatment claims – as well as giving me plenty of opportunities to scare my boyfriend by sneaking up on him wearing each one.

Only masks that use the brightest, flicker-free bulbs, fit comfortably and are easy to use made the final cut. After testing, I returned the masks sourced for this article to the manufacturers. Where that wasn’t possible, I cleaned the masks and donated them to the Redbridge Reach Out service, which supports anyone experiencing domestic abuse.
What we loveFully customisable; particularly good for anti-ageing
What we don’t loveIts high price and bulky controller

Most LED masks come with a few settings that treat the entire face for one skin concern. But many of us don’t have uniform faces: a dark spot here, a blemish there, fine lines elsewhere. One flat treatment might help with overall skin condition, but it can’t pinpoint a specific skin concern exactly where you need it.

The CurrentBody Series 3 is the only mask I’ve found that allows users to completely customise their treatments. It’s also the only mask I’ve tested that offers penetrating deep near-infrared lights across the whole face, making it the new LED mask to beat.

Why we love it The mask has 125 light points spread over the face, each of which can produce six light wavelengths: green for pigmentation, yellow for redness, blue for blemishes, red for wrinkles, near-infrared for firming and near-infrared to support deeper skin renewal. I was able to select exactly which light (or combination of lights) I wanted to shine from each light point on the face using the CurrentBody app. Since I primarily get spots on my chin, I targeted these breakouts while sticking to anti-ageing treatments elsewhere and threw in some yellow light to tackle redness in my cheeks.

I usually hate apps for beauty tech, but I found it refreshingly simple to use, without any ads or pop-ups. Tailoring the light colours I wanted was as easy as using a colouring book, and the app then automatically programmed the light levels to ensure the right dosage within the 10-minute treatment time. It paired seamlessly with the mask to run my custom treatment – the whole process took less than five minutes.

In terms of results, the redness in my cheeks had faded, my chin appeared to clear quickly after a particularly brutal hormonal breakout, and the rest of my skin looked glowier and healthier than usual after my six weeks of testing. And, if you aren’t fussed about personalising your treatments, the mask has four pre-programmed options for anti-ageing, blemishes, redness and dark spots.

It’s a shame that … it’s so expensive and, to accommodate its wider range of treatment options, its controller has a touchscreen that’s frustratingly easy to knock to pause or stop your treatment midway.

Number of LEDs: 750 at 125 light points Number of settings: four preset, with unlimited customisation Treatment time: 10mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm), blue (415nm), green (532nm), yellow (590nm) Timer countdown: yes
Read our full CurrentBody Series 3 LED mask review for more details
What we loveFully customisable; particularly good for anti-ageing
What we don’t loveIts high price and bulky controller
What we loveComfortable to use; good colour choices; accessible price
What we don’t loveFewer bulbs than higher-end models and no near-infrared

If you want to try light therapy without remortgaging the house, the Silk’n LED face mask 100 is a good choice. It has 100 LED bulbs with good facial coverage, is comfortable to wear, and offers a good range of light colours. It doesn’t have near-infrared lights like the pricier options, but it covers the basics at a decent price.

Why we love it This mask offers four colour modes: red, blue, yellow and purple. Red light helps stimulate collagen to reduce the appearance of fine lines, while blue light helps to soothe breakouts. The purple light comes from mixing the aforementioned blue and red lights, combining the effects of both to boost the skin’s overall evenness.

Although less widely researched (and with limited clinical evidence to suggest efficacy), the experts I spoke to said the yellow-light treatment could help improve hydration levels in the skin. I didn’t notice a huge hydration hit when testing this feature, so if your skin is crying out for hydration, I recommend using the other light settings alongside a hydrating serum.
Each colour can be selected individually for a 10-minute targeted session, or you can select automatic mode, which cycles through the colours over 15 minutes to provide all the benefits at once.

I found the Silk’n light therapy mask simple to use and comfortable to wear. Its flexible silicone build didn’t feel quite as sturdy as more expensive options, but I didn’t really notice this when using the mask. The built-in eye shields weren’t as bulky as others, but they still blocked out the light and protected my eyes well.
The automatic mode left my skin feeling completely comfortable, with a slightly glowier finish than usual – just what I’d expect from an entry-level mask such as this one.

It’s a shame that … there’s no timer and it has fewer than a seventh of the bulbs of the CurrentBody, with no near-infrared light treatment for effective collagen stimulation deeper in the skin. This means it’s better for light-touch anti-ageing, and for soothing, acne-busting blue-light treatments.
Number of LEDs: 100 Number of settings: five Treatment time: 10 or 15mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), purple (463nm+633nm), blue (463nm), yellow (592nm) Timer countdown: no
What we loveComfortable to use; good colour choices; accessible price
What we don’t loveFewer bulbs than higher-end models and no near-infrared
What we loveFull facial coverage with simple cordless controls
What we don’t loveMask steams up a little inside and there’s no countdown

Most face masks look a little creepy, but the TheraFace Mask Glo takes this to another level. It focuses on providing full facial coverage over the mouth and nose area, and its glowing red eyes might be the last thing you’d want to see staring back at you from across a dark room, but the results are fantastic. And, if its appearance gives you a shock, you can switch on its massage function to calm back down.

Why we love it The first thing to note about the TheraFace Mask Glo is its sturdy build, which feels surprisingly lightweight on the face thanks to the adjustable back and top straps and large silicone-padded eye area. These distribute the weight across the brow bone and undereyes and around the head so that everything feels comfortable, no matter the position you’re in. There’s also a removable inner eye insert that blocks light from your eyes without blocking light from reaching the undereye area, where it can help reduce the appearance of fine lines.

The mask has 168 light points that emit the three most well-researched light wavelengths: blue, red and near-infrared light. These can be selected as individual settings, or you can kick back while the automatic 12-minute treatment cycles through everything you need to target fine lines, firmness and breakout-causing bacteria. Alongside this, I found the steady vibration massage, located in the mask’s straps, oddly relaxing. Its aim is to gently stimulate the scalp, increase circulation and relieve tension, but if you find the massage uncomfortable, it can be switched off.

Another selling point is its wireless controls. It has two buttons, which scroll through the three treatment modes and the vibration massage functions. These are intuitive, and I liked that I could roam around freely instead of carrying around a wired controller for the 12-minute treatment.
It’s a shame that … its lack of mouth and nose holes means the mask steams up by the end of a session. Also, it doesn’t have a countdown, so the 12-minute treatment can feel long.

Number of LEDs: 504 at 168 light points Number of settings: three LED modes, plus an automatic cycle, and three massage functions Treatment time: 4-12mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm) Timer countdown: no
What we loveFull facial coverage with simple cordless controls
What we don’t loveMask steams up a little inside and there’s no countdown
What we loveTargeted blemish treatments in a portable package
What we don’t loveLeech-like appearance and extra running cost

Acne can be a real pain, and many cosmetic treatments that target it leave skin feeling irritated, dry and flaky. These nifty adhesive LED patches from Lustre use blue light, which the company claims reduces breakout-causing bacteria.

Why we love it Each Solo patch has 15 pure blue LEDs at the proven wavelength for treating acne, 415nm. The patches cover a targeted area of skin about 2.5 x 5cm, which is perfect for treating problem areas such as the chin, cheeks and forehead. Since they’re rechargeable and far smaller than a typical LED face mask, they’re highly portable, making it easy to stick to a treatment routine.
I found the targeted treatments very effective for minimising breakouts in my chin area – somewhere I often struggle with spots. Continued treatments saw fewer breakouts and faster healing.

The patches come with a supply of double-sided adhesive to fix each one to your skin, allowing you to move around freely during treatment. This also means, unlike typical light therapy masks, they can be safely fixed anywhere on the body.

If you’re worried that the adhesive will feel uncomfortable or be tricky to remove from breakouts, don’t be. The patches are so lightweight that the adhesive doesn’t need to be very strong. I found it easy and comfortable to peel off the patches after the recommended 20-minute treatment time.

It’s a shame that … you need to buy the sticky patches when they run out. These cost £18 for a pack of 60, or 30p each. They also look a bit like leeches – only you can decide if that’s more palatable than the Hannibal Lecter look of the full-face LED masks.
Number of LEDs: 15 Number of settings: one Treatment time: 20mins Light wavelengths: blue (415nm) Timer countdown: no
What we loveTargeted blemish treatments in a portable package
What we don’t loveLeech-like appearance and extra running cost
What we loveComfortable fit; wireless controls; fast treatments
What we don’t loveImperfect eye shielding and fiddly straps

Most LED masks recommend 10- to 15-minute daily treatments for best results. If you’re short on time but still want to invest in a reliable face mask, the SpectraLite FaceWare Pro is my recommendation. It offers anti-ageing, anti-blemish and a combination of both treatments, with daily sessions taking just three minutes. That’s something even the most time-poor can commit to, and consistency is what gets you results.

Why we love it This is the most comfortable hard-shell LED mask I’ve tested. It’s lined with a thick, flexible but sturdy-feeling layer of silicone that provides cushioning on every part of the face. During use, it evenly distributed the mask’s weight across my nose, forehead and cheekbones, no matter if I was lying flat or sitting up.

I was surprised by this, since the mask’s battery is built into the forehead rather than in a separate remote – the Lustre Renew Pro Facewear reviewed below has a similar design but is less comfortable to wear. The SpectraLite FaceWare Pro perfects the hands-free design, making it comfortable, breathable and easy to control with one button. Mercifully, there’s no useless app.

In the mask, you’ll find 100 red LEDs (including red, near-infrared and amber) and 62 blue LEDs distributed over 80 light points on the face. These have been strategically positioned so that the blue lights cover the nose, forehead, chin and lower cheeks (oily areas where acne-causing bacteria thrive), while the red light is more evenly dispersed. There are separate red anti-ageing and blue acne-fighting modes, but I used the combination mode in my tests and was pleasantly surprised by how well the mask reduced blemishes while easing redness across my face.

The keen-eyed among you may notice that the three-minute treatments are significantly shorter than the 10- to 20-minute treatment times recommended by the experts I spoke with. However, according to the brand, its clinical studies have seen results from red-light treatments within 10 weeks of daily use, and blue light within two weeks. In my weeks testing this mask, my skin did appear smoother, brighter and clearer. If you’re hunting for a quick, comfortable mask without fancy features, such as app connectivity and additional colour options, this is a strong bet.

It’s a shame that … its straps aren’t the easiest to adjust, and the mask doesn’t shield the eyes as effectively as others. If you have sensitive eyes, opt for something that has built-in eye guards instead. It also doesn’t have a remote or a countdown, but the treatments are so quick that this isn’t much of an issue.
Number of LEDs: 162 Number of settings: three Treatment time: 3mins Light wavelengths: red (630nm), amber (605nm), near-infrared (880nm), blue (415nm) Timer countdown: no
What we loveComfortable fit; wireless controls; fast treatments
What we don’t loveImperfect eye shielding and fiddly straps
What we loveDeep NIR light at a sensible price, with a handy travel case
What we don’t loveConfusing settings and a finicky fit

For a long time, deep near-infrared light was reserved for the most expensive LED masks. So, when the Silk’n LED face mask Pro launched in October 2025, with 20 deep near-infrared lights included on the forehead and around the eyes and mouth, I was keen to try it. Even more so when I learned of its comparatively reasonable price.

While its treatments aren’t quite as streamlined as the CurrentBody Series 3 above, it offers a range of treatments and light wavelengths at half the cost. So, if you want a great value mask, or travel often and need a mask that packs down well, this is my recommendation.

Why we love it This mask packs in seven treatment options, which combine five wavelengths of light. A few of these treatments felt a little surplus to requirements, such as the stand-alone red- or amber-light treatments – I can’t fathom why you wouldn’t want to use the setting that includes near-infrared and deep near-infrared as well. But the treatments I used most often were effective. The red-light settings had a good calming effect on my skin, and when I paired this with a few minutes of the blue light, I noticed my blemishes reduced and healed faster.

All the controls for this mask are built into a small battery pack, which magnetically attaches to the front of the mask. While this means you don’t get to see a countdown or a screen displaying setting time, there are no wires to mess around with. The battery is incredibly lightweight and can last through a whole week of treatments without recharging.

I also liked this mask’s flexible straps and its adjustable chin strap. The Silk’n Pro packs down completely flat or folds into its carry case, not much larger than a box of tissues, for travel. This is incredibly useful if you’re frequently away from home.

It’s a shame that … the chin strap hangs away from the chin slightly, and I found the eye guards pressed hard into the bridge of my nose. I also found it confusing to select different treatments because the various configurations of red-toned light were indistinguishable from each other.

Number of LEDs: 480 at 120 light points Number of settings: seven Treatment time: 10mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm), blue (463nm), amber (605nm) Timer countdown: no
What we loveDeep NIR light at a sensible price, with a handy travel case
What we don’t loveConfusing settings and a finicky fit
What we loveIntuitive to use; targeted treatments; undereye cooling
What we don’t loveHeavy mask that presses into the undereyes when reclining

The Shark CryoGlow is the only LED face mask I’ve tested that offers built-in undereye cooling alongside targeted light therapy. It has three different wavelengths of light: blue, red and near-infrared, arranged into presets for “better ageing”, “blemish repair” and “skin sustain”. I found the lights incredibly bright during my tests – although for safety, they automatically dim when you remove the mask from your face – but I was happy with how the mask shielded my eyes.

During every treatment, you can choose to switch on the cooling undereye patches, which aim to de-puff and soothe your skin. The cooling can also be used on its own, without the LEDs. There are three levels, the coolest of which felt startlingly cold at first but did a great job of calming down my eyes on a particularly bad hay fever day. Likewise, the blemish mode did a brilliant job of calming spots and redness with sustained use. I also liked using the skin sustain mode for a quick pick-me-up to brighten skin before a night out.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s noticeably heavier than its silicone competitors, and other plastic masks that don’t have undereye cooling. The mask fits comfortably when you’re sitting up, but when lying down, the metal cooling patches pressed into the delicate area under my eyes. Similarly, the location of the cooling patches means the light can’t access fine lines under the eyes. Another unfortunate side-effect of the cooling is the whirring noise it makes – inaudible from far away, but pretty noisy when pressed on to your face. I think most people would be better off with the TheraFace Mask Glo.

Number of LEDs: 160; number of settings: four; treatment time: 4-8mins light therapy; 5-15mins undereye cooling; light wavelengths: red (630nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm); timer countdown: yes
What we loveIntuitive to use; targeted treatments; undereye cooling
What we don’t loveHeavy mask that presses into the undereyes when reclining
What we loveExcellent coverage; comfortable; deep near-infrared lights
What we don’t loveOnly one treatment mode; no screen to display treatment time

If the multiple settings in the Series 3 mask above offer more versatility than you’ll use, and you’re mainly hoping to achieve anti-ageing results, choose this mask. The CurrentBody Series 2 mask was my top choice on this page for a long time, and it’s still an incredibly comfortable, effective mask that offers red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared lights.

The deep near-infrared lights penetrate deeper than the other two types of light, CurrentBody claims. This leads to more effective treatment where it’s needed most – the deep near-infrared bulbs are positioned under the eyes and around the lips to better target areas where ageing is more pronounced.

I used this mask for three months, and was pleased to notice my skin looking calmer and more even-toned than usual, with less undereye inflammation. As it’s a red-light mask, it didn’t have much effect on my acne, but it did help to reduce redness.

It didn’t make the final cut because … as someone with temperamental skin, I think spending the extra £100 on the multiuse Series 3 is worth it. This mask offers only one treatment setting, and there isn’t a screen displaying the treatment time. Neither is a dealbreaker, but it’s nice to be able to choose different treatments, and at this price, I’d expect a countdown timer.
Number of LEDs: 236; number of settings: one; treatment time: 10mins; light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm); timer countdown: no
What we loveExcellent coverage; comfortable; deep near-infrared lights
What we don’t loveOnly one treatment mode; no screen to display treatment time
What we loveAdjustable design and versatile settings
What we don’t loveLess close contact with the chin area

The neck and decollete are often the first places to show signs of ageing, as the skin is thinner in those areas. Consequently, expensive neck light therapy masks have started to flood the market – but rather than requiring additional expensive kit, this Stylpro mask can be adjusted to treat multiple areas including the back, neck, scalp and face.

It’s incredibly versatile. It has red, deep red, near-infrared and blue light, which all combine into 11 programs to target different areas of concern on your body. The remote control has a huge screen, making it easy to select the desired programme and treatment zone. This also displays the mask’s battery life and treatment time.

In my tests, the straps did a great job of keeping the flexible silicone mask in place. Its eye shields were also brilliant at blocking out light, and the snap fasteners made it easy to adjust the mask between different treatment areas. To treat the back and neck area, I found you needed to lie down or sit up very straight to prevent it from slipping, but it was great to have the versatility.

It didn’t make the final cut because … when used in face mode, the mask hangs a few inches away from the chin area, which means the light has less direct contact there. Its eye guards also tended to gently pinch the bridge of my nose.
Number of LEDs: 137; number of settings: 11; treatment time: 12-15mins; light wavelengths: red (633nm), deep red (655nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm); timer countdown: yes
What we loveAdjustable design and versatile settings
What we don’t loveLess close contact with the chin area
What we loveApp control for personalised treatments
What we don’t loveLess comfortable to wear

Most light treatment masks have wired controls. That doesn’t mean you need to remain tethered to a single spot, but it does mean there’s a remote that you have to carry around with you. This mask from Lustre, on the other hand, is controlled via a mobile app. The two preset treatments can also be operated using a button on the mask.

It has two programmes, called Energise and Revitalise, and uses blue, red and near-infrared light. Unusually, you can choose which kind of light you want to use in four areas of your face: forehead, eyes, nose, and cheeks and chin. In my tests, I liked being able to treat spots on my chin with blue light while using red light on the rest of my face.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not very comfortable. Since the battery is on the mask itself, it’s a little top heavy, and the eye protectors don’t do a great job of shielding your eyes.
Also, I hate having lots of apps on my phone – it’s up to you whether the wireless freedom is worth the app installation.

Number of LEDs: 80; number of settings: two presets, with in-app personalisation options across four facial zones; treatment time: 10mins; light wavelengths: red (630nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm); timer countdown: yes
What we loveApp control for personalised treatments
What we don’t loveLess comfortable to wear
What we loveDeep near-infrared light and concentrated treatment
What we don’t loveLess comfortable to wear than a mask

If your main area of concern is the lip area, you might not need to buy a full mask. The Silk’n LumiLips has 30 LEDs concentrated in the lip area, covering smile lines and the chin. It has five light wavelengths – amber, red, dark red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared. The only other masks in this roundup offering deep near-infrared light are more than £250, which gives you a good idea of how much value it offers.

The mask has two modes, both of which use dark red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared light. The red-light mode claims to promote lip volume and firmness, while the second mode adds in amber light to reduce pigmentation and redness. I love that the mask requires only a five-minute daily treatment, making its less-than-comfortable mouthpiece slightly more bearable.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s built like an adult pacifier and feels like one too. You have to bite down on the mouthpiece to keep it in place, which is far less comfortable than just wearing a mask with a strap around your head.

Number of LEDs: 30; number of settings: two; treatment time: 5mins; light wavelengths: amber (605nm), red (633nm), dark red (660nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm); timer countdown: no
What we loveDeep near-infrared light and concentrated treatment
What we don’t loveLess comfortable to wear than a mask
What we loveDedicated, soothing treatment for eye area
What we don’t loveSmall LED light coverage
Best for: reviving and soothing the undereyes

LED face masks usually arrive with guards to protect your eyes from the light, which means they neglect to treat the delicate skin around the eyes – an area particularly prone to fine lines, wrinkles and discoloration.

The Peep Club heated eye wand is a nifty little gadget that was designed in collaboration with optometrists, primarily as a hot compress to help with dry, tired eyes. The LED+ model includes a small LED light, which glows red to reduce fine lines and amber to decrease the visible blood vessels that cause dark circles. There’s also green light for soothing inflammation, although the evidence around green light is shaky.

During testing, I found it soothed my irritated eyes after long days staring at a screen. The amber light setting seemed to reduce my dark circles, too, after a few weeks of consistent use. As recommended, I used it with the Peep Club coconut eye balm to give the wand a bit of slip, which avoided irritating the delicate skin under my eyes.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not as convenient to use as a dedicated mask, since you have to glide it over the skin. Its LED light is small, so you need to dedicate a lot of time to treatment to get the best results. While I love using the coconut eye balm and a 40ml tub lasts a long time, it leaves an oily slip on the skin after treatment, and the need for this extra running cost may be off-putting.
Number of LEDs: not listed; number of settings: five, three with LED; treatment time: 5mins; light wavelengths: amber (605nm), red (633nm), green (525nm); timer countdown: yes
What we loveDedicated, soothing treatment for eye area
What we don’t loveSmall LED light coverage

I’ve tested many more LED devices than can fit on this page, and while I don’t usually draw attention to bad products, I came across so many poorly designed models that I feel it necessary to shed light on the LED masks that overpromise and underdeliver.

First, we have the Revolution Pro Miracle LED face mask, which costs just £59.99 at full price. Believe me, I wanted this mask to be a winner, but its solid plastic structure, with no eye shielding or padding, made it so wildly uncomfortable to wear that it was an almost instant write-off. The straps are another problem; they come together around the bottom part of your head, causing the mask to constantly fall. It also seems built for very small faces, so it constantly slipped down my face, pinching my nose and making it difficult to breathe properly – even if I used it without the straps and lay flat during treatment. Throw in fewer LED bulbs than average and dim lights, and this mask is impossible to recommend.

A high price tag doesn’t guarantee how good the mask is either, as evidenced by the Foreo FAQ 202 LED mask, £719 at full price. Its light weight and comfort level, along with an array of treatment options via its app-based controls, meant it impressed initially. However, its silicone design felt incredibly flimsy, and after a week of use, it had already started peeling away from the central battery pack.

This might be forgivable if Foreo offered a full warranty and repair service. There’s a two-year warranty covering defects and faulty workmanship, but this does not cover “cosmetic deterioration caused by fair wear and tear, or damage caused by accident, misuse or neglect”. To access accidental damage coverage, you have to pay Foreo’s £9.99/month subscription. Even if you’re happy to risk it, at the time of testing in June 2026, you still had to shell out £4.99/month to access the mask’s full suite of preset treatments. Add to this the scale of advertising you’re bombarded with in the app – some of it unskippable. When you consider its price, this brazen money-grubbing leaves a very bad taste.

Through testing this family of devices, I had also been hoping to find an undereye brightening LED patch to usurp the Peep Club wand, which requires constant movement across the eye area. I had hoped that the Lustre GoGlow brightening and de-puffing patches would fit the bill. They come in a handy headphone-like charging case and have a clever wireless design. However, when positioned under the eyes as advertised, the light was incredibly bright, which made it tricky to see. The sticky pads, although small, were uncomfortable to remove, and my skin was left feeling irritated for a day afterwards. The search for the perfect undereye LED patch continues …

“LED (light-emitting diode) therapy is a non-invasive treatment that uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate various cellular processes in the skin,” says aesthetic medicine expert Kubicka. “Depending on the colour or wavelength, LED light can target inflammation, promote collagen production, accelerate healing and even kill bacteria.”

Light therapy is a great addition to your skincare routine – for me, it’s helped reduce breakouts, improve healing and reduce the appearance of my acne scars. LED face masks are quick, gentle and non-invasive, and suitable for most skin types (although as mentioned above, blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, according to the experts I spoke with). The masks are effective and foolproof to use, and the daily treatments also force you to take a little time for yourself – perfect for a morning pick-me-up or an evening wind-down.

“Red-light therapy can reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles through a process called photobiomodulation,” says consultant dermatologist Phillips. “It energises mitochondria, which are the batteries of the cells, powering the production of collagen and elastin by fibroblasts, the factories of the skin.”

Elastin and collagen are “the building blocks of firm, youthful skin”, says Kubicka. Stimulating the production of these molecules can “improve skin density, elasticity and overall smoothness” as long as you complete treatments regularly.

I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles, but I’m keen to avoid more by using red-light therapy for “preventive ageing”. However, “most of the clinical evidence focuses on treating visible signs of ageing or repairing damaged skin, rather than long-term prevention in younger skin”, as aesthetic doctor Verma explains.

Still, Verma reassured me my efforts wouldn’t be in vain. “Using LED light consistently and appropriately may help support overall skin health […] especially when combined with sun protection and a good skincare routine.”
For more, read do you really need an LED face mask?
Several colours are available, with each wavelength said to target a different skin concern. These colours correlate to the visible light spectrum, and each can have a different effect on the skin.

Red light has a wavelength of between 630 and 700nm and is the most widely known form of light therapy, loved for its non-invasive potential anti-ageing benefits. Near-infrared light above 700nm “penetrates the skin more deeply to support tissue repair and reduce inflammation”, according to Kubicka. Blue-light therapy (415nm), on the other hand, has been proven to target acne-causing bacteria, leading to a reduction in breakouts over time. Kubicka also says blue light can help regulate oil production – another common problem for those with acne.

The effects of some types of light on the skin are better researched than others. Near-infrared, red light and blue light are backed by scientific studies that identify the biological processes that each type of light triggers in the body.

Meanwhile, research into green and yellow light is more limited. One study questions the efficacy of yellow-light therapy and claims that a previous study may have been influenced by the placebo effect. Similarly, a study on green light therapy suggests that more research is needed to provide a solid recommendation for use as an anti-ageing treatment.
The “how” is simple: always use light therapy masks on freshly washed, dry skin, before applying serums and creams. This will give the light the most direct access to the skin.

Despite what some instruction manuals advise, don’t jump into daily treatments straight away – you may end up with slightly irritated skin. Start by introducing treatments two to three times a week, and monitoring the impact on your skin. If you don’t notice any sensitivity, you can incorporate more treatments, if permitted by the manufacturer’s guidelines.

Once your skin is used to the treatment, “home devices should be used three to five times a week, for 10-20 minutes a session,” says Phillips. But treatment times vary between devices, so always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and don’t expect instant results. If you’re hoping to reduce breakouts, you should “see a reduction in redness and the frequency of acne breakouts within two to four weeks”. Those using red light for anti-ageing benefits will need to wait a little longer: “It typically takes six to eight weeks to see visible changes.”

“LED light therapy is generally very safe when used correctly,” says Verma. This is because, unlike laser hair removal, it only uses low-level, non-thermal light. “The most common side effects are mild and temporary, such as slight redness, dryness or irritation.”

“People with known photosensitive disorders or taking medications that make them more sensitive to light (eg certain antibiotics) should consult their doctor,” says Phillips. He also warns that those with darker skin tones should exercise caution when using blue light, since “some blue wavelengths have been associated with hyperpigmentation”. The Lustre Solo patches recommended above offer exclusively blue light, but the other masks in this roundup have blue-light-free settings if you do find that it causes sensitivity.

There are hundreds of light therapy masks available at different prices, but the quality varies wildly. You may see results from a budget-friendly mask, such as the Silk’n LED face mask 100 reviewed above, but spending more will generally get you a larger quantity of bulbs that offer a greater range of wavelengths. You’re also more likely to get a mask with a better fit and coverage.

The best mask for you will depend on your skin concerns and budget. Those hoping to invest in a mask with anti-acne properties will be able to spend less, since blue light is more widely available, but if you’re looking for the best anti-ageing deep near-infrared light therapy, you will need to part with more cash.
High-end red-light therapy masks can cost upwards of £500; if you spend that much, just make sure you use it regularly, or you won’t see results.

Cleaning instructions for LED masks will differ slightly from brand to brand, based on the different materials used. As a general rule, you want to steer clear of using chemical or alcohol-based cleansers since these can damage a mask’s delicate silicone and padded components. Always check the instructions for your specific mask before jumping into cleaning.

The usual best practice is to use a non-abrasive cloth, such as microfibre, dampened with water to wipe down your mask after every use. Try not to use too much water and never submerge the mask, as doing so will damage the electrical components. Always make sure your mask is unplugged and switched off before cleaning, and wait for the mask to dry completely before storing, charging or switching it on.

For more: The best concealers for camouflaging blemishes The best retinol and retinal serums for smoother, firmer skin The best eye creams for banishing bags, puffiness and fine lines Shark FacialPro Glow + DePuffi review

Sarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)

items.title: Norman Foster creates first-ever watch in collaboration with Lebond
paragraphs: British architect Norman Foster has unveiled his first watch, designed with watch brand Lebond in a process he said was “very similar to architecture.”
The mechanical watch has a sleek silhouette with an integrated strap. According to Foster, the design process began with a reevaluation of what we assume a watch should look like.
“We wanted to look again at something very familiar and reconsider it as a complete object, with the case, the strap, the dial and the movement all part of a system,” Foster told Dezeen.

“Normally, you have a watch case and then you attach a strap to it. We started to question the obvious. Why should they feel like two separate objects? Once we began thinking of the strap as a continuation of the case, the whole watch started to come together.”
As a result, the Lebond Norman Foster has a 38.5-millimetre-wide Grade 5 titanium case that widens to 40 millimetres where it connects to the integrated strap, creating a streamlined design.
The architect also got rid of the traditional watch lugs, wrapping the strap around the timepiece’s titanium case instead.
“Removing the conventional lugs gave us the continuous profile, but it also made the watch more comfortable and more integrated,” Foster explained.
The Lebond Norman Foster, with its distinctive rotor, also evokes aviation design – a reference to Foster’s interest in flying, as well as to his history of international travel.
This comes across in a very practical way, with the watch’s bidirectional rotating 12-hour bezel allowing the wearer to read a second time zone using the main hour hand.
Its dial is protected by a domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating, and the watch is water-resistant to 50 metres.

It is currently available in two versions: the Natural Titanium Edition, which has a micro-sandblasted titanium case, a brushed-metal dial and a grey rubber strap, and the Black Edition, which features a matte black DLC-coated titanium case matched with a black lacquered dial and hands and a black rubber strap.
Foster designed the watch to allow people to customise it, swapping cases and straps at will, and more versions will be released over time.

“A watch is intensely personal. You wear it, you travel with it and it becomes part of your everyday life,” Foster said. “This led to the potential for a wide range of colour combinations and the ability to customise the watch”
“By designing an easy attachment mechanism, the user is able to interchange elements and create personal versions,” he continued.

“I proposed a watch that could move naturally between very different situations, working in the studio, being on a building site, travelling or going somewhere formal. It should not feel precious or limited to one particular setting.”
This marks the first time that Foster, who is known as the most successful architect in history, has designed a watch, but he didn’t find the process daunting.

“I have never really thought that scale changes the nature of design,” Foster said. “Whether it is a city, a building, a chair or a watch, you are still asking the same questions: how does it work, how is it made, and how do all the parts come together?”
“The process is also very similar to architecture,” he continued.

“It becomes one of refinement, sketches, prototypes, adjustments and then more adjustments. You explore options to finally arrive at the essential idea and then you keep refining it until everything seems inevitable.”
Last year, in celebration of Foster’s 90th birthday, we looked at twelve defining projects from his long career. Next month, the architect will give the keynote speech at the Dezeen Awards party.

items.title: The bare-handed beekeeper who looks like something out of The Odyssey: Holly Lynton’s best photograph
paragraphs: The jumping-off point for my Bare Handed series was a bird becoming trapped in the netting around the raspberry bushes in my backyard. It made me think of the problem humans have interacting with the natural world. How do we navigate obtaining food and the other things we need while still being good stewards of the land? I’d seen work by photographers demonstrating how Big Agriculture was destroying the environment. I wanted to find people who took a respectful approach, tried to work in tandem with it, but who might be in a fearful or dangerous situation.

I approached Les, the man in this picture, after speaking to the director of an exhibition space in Albuquerque, New Mexico, who had hired him to remove a feral beehive from his tree. I’d already tried to photograph another beekeeper who wore a full protective suit, but he might as well have been an astronaut. With Les, I was able to stay nearby and work with him over three days. The first couple involved straightforward documentary pictures of him tending his hives. Then, on the third day, his apprentice Amber showed up to help.

Les had the queen bee in a cage in his shirt pocket and asked Amber to take it out. Wherever the queen is, the rest of the colony will swarm. There’s a picture I made where Les and Amber are joined together by bees, and that was my “ah ha!” moment. Amber took out the queen and placed her in Les’s hand, which is where the bees went next. He looked at me with his hands full of bees and said: “Should I put them on my face?” I said: “Sure!”

Les slowly moved his hands up to his face. Bees don’t like hair, which is why they’re not in his beard or the top of his head. He closed his eyes for a few minutes, and I photographed. Afterwards, he said: “You know, I couldn’t hear anything but the buzzing.” I don’t think he’d ever done that before. People sometimes have their own ideas, which I just go with. One of the reasons I like spending some time with them is that when they’re engaged in work, it’s almost like watching a dance and waiting for the right gesture.

Les didn’t wear gloves when handling the bees. He said he needed to be able to feel them so he didn’t crush them, and that it was too hot to wear a suit. I wore a shirt that buttoned up tight at the wrists and tried wearing a beekeeper’s veil, too, but I abandoned that after finding it hard to focus through the mesh. I did get a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up.

I was using a medium-format analogue camera, and the bees were also landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see them. That was disconcerting, but Les advised me just to move slowly, as he did. That worked: I didn’t get stung.

For a while, the photograph of Amber and Les joined together by bees was the one I preferred. I was worried people would find the bees on his face over the top. The themes of the project were quickly reinforced when I photographed wolves in a sanctuary with their trainers, and then went out with a family of catfish noodlers in rural Oklahoma. “Noodling” involved them catching these fish with their bare hands – even though they can weigh 45kg and really fight back. I realised none of these people had any fear. They were all experts at whatever it was they were doing, and for them this was a spiritual, meditative practice. That became the focus for the series.

Before I started taking photography classes, I planned to be a psychologist and a writer. But what I love about photography is that you can create ambiguous narratives, a multilayered story in a single frame. A lot of my work references cultural memory. Rather than straight documentary, I’m aiming for something more mythic, and gestures that happen spontaneously can sometimes seem to reference a certain myth or biblical allusion. This photograph leans more towards Greek mythology, even if it doesn’t directly reference an exact story. Les isn’t Odysseus but, like him, he elects to hear rather than protect himself, which makes him feel like he’s a part of The Odyssey, somehow.

High point: High points occur when my photographs are both made and shown. When photographing, a high point is when everything aligns – the light, content, composition – and I create an unanticipated image that transcends the moment. One that elicits allusion, mystery and wonder. In terms of exhibitions or publications, it’s often what is recent. In the past few years, institutions as varied as the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City and Bristol Cathedral in England have exhibited my work. I’m thankful that institutions have enabled people from many different backgrounds and perspectives to see my photographs. Talking with viewers and hearing their reactions has been a real gift. My book Bare Handed, published by L’Artiere, was another high point.

Top tip: Right now, the quest for authenticity instead of artifice feels crucial, and what I’d urge photographers to undertake. I’d also say there is no such thing as too much curiosity (even though some people might make you think so). Don’t be afraid to change your mind about what you are working on, the meaning behind it or how to go about it. Reframing is what I like to call it. Follow your intuition. And find the joy in the practice of making work and being creative. Difficult moments will occur, and ones that feel like failures, but it’s the journey, not the end goal.

items.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
paragraphs: Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

items.title: AI drones help farmers and the planet – level 1
paragraphs: Weeds are wild plants. They grow in fields. Farmers do not want them in their fields.

Farmers use a lot of chemicals. These chemicals kill weeds. But chemicals are not good for nature. Most farming machines are big and expensive. They work only a little bit every year. Another problem is that most chemicals end up in soil and on plants. This way of farming is expensive and it does not work very well.
One company makes drones. These drones use AI. The drones fly over fields. They find weeds. They spray only weeds. This saves money and the planet, too. The drones save 95% of chemicals.
Difficult words: chemical (a substance which does not come from nature), soil (the brown substance in which plants grow), drone (a small flying vehicle which a person operates).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: AI drones help farmers and the planet – level 2
paragraphs: Farmers need to deal with weeds in a more environmentally friendly way. Global warming makes weeds grow faster which means that farmers must use more chemicals.

The surprising fact is that 95% of these chemicals go into the soil or they end up on plants. Spraying fields is expensive and very inefficient. Startups like Precision AI are introducing a fresh approach with AI-powered drones which reduce chemical use by up to 90%. Traditional farming uses expensive machines like ground sprayers, which cost a lot and farmers use them only a few weeks a year. Precision AI uses AI drones which scan fields, check plant types, and spray only the weeds. This saves about 95% of chemicals compared to old methods.

Difficult words: weed (a wild plant which grows where people do not want it), approach (the way of dealing with a problem or situation), inefficient (a person, system, or machine that does not work in the best way and wastes money, time or energy).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: AI drones help farmers and the planet – level 3
paragraphs: The urgent need to combat weeds sustainably has been heightened by global warming, which accelerates their growth, posing a threat to crops and food security.

Traditional methods involve excessive chemical spraying, resulting in environmental harm. Startups like Precision AI are introducing innovative solutions, such as AI-enabled crop-spraying drones, which reduce chemical usage by up to 90%. These drones employ AI to precisely identify plant species in real-time, allowing targeted chemical applications to eliminate weeds while minimizing environmental impact.

Currently, a significant portion of chemicals applied in agriculture goes to waste. Precision AI aims to shift the industry towards a ‘spray as a service’ model, leveraging precision farming technologies. Despite the potential benefits, challenges include navigating international regulations, scaling up the technology, and addressing concerns about job displacement due to autonomous farming.
Difficult words: heighten (to make or become more intense), leverage (to use borrowed money for investments), scale up (to increase something in size, number, or extent).

items.title: Flokk's design-forward seating features on Dezeen Showroom
paragraphs: From distinctive task chairs to sprawling modular systems, the following seating has been released this year by Scandinavian furniture manufacturer Flokk‘s sub-brands.

The HÅG X Recouture Capisco task chair features the original HÅG Capisco task chair’s distinctive cruciform backrest, developed by designer Peter Opsvik and originally released by Flokk-owned ergonomic chair brand HÅG in 1984.

In the this version, created in collaboration with textiles brand Recouture, the rear side of the backrest is upholstered in traditional Norwegian vintage åkle textile, characterised by bright colours and scintillating patterns.

Users can select from various base colour and finish options, while the åkle material itself is vintage, meaning that each is one of a kind and is matched with a complementary block-coloured wool upholstery covering the seat.
Design studio Webb has created an flexible, snaking sofa system for Flokk-owned, UK-based furniture brand Connection.
Terrain modular seating comes in various colourways and module options, which can be reconfigured to facilitate relaxation and informal meetings in across lobbies, workplaces and education interiors.
An enveloping, tub-like shape characterises this cosy seat produced for Connection by Italian duo Lucidi Pevere.
Contrast manifests in the Oko chair where its upholstered base and plump cushioning meet a sleek, curved read panel made from wood.
Connection has also released a modular sofa named Leo, created by Turkish interior designers Km34, who included sprung seats and matching feather-filled arm pillows for a sense of old-world comfort.
Its slender metal legs and base give it a contemporary aesthetic, as do its rectilinear side panels and cushions, which come in a range of bright and neutral colourways.
HÅG Minu was conceived by Norwegian designers Andreas Engesvik and Jannicke Grung for HÅG with the aim of bringing the comfort and playfulness of residential furniture to workplaces.
Made from up to 60 per cent recycled materials, the chair has a compact form available in seven designer-curated curated colourways, with further customisation options available upon request.
Flokk is a family of 11 design brands that specialise in ergonomic chairs, seats and modular systems geared specifically for use in workplaces.
Through its products, the brands aim to foster health, wellbeing, productivity and sustainability for users, while enhancing interiors with design-forward seating solutions.

items.title: Joe & Mac Retro Collection (Switch 2) review: the '90s caveman roundup inherits its flaws as well as its fun
paragraphs: A better collection than its headline game suggests. The original Joe & Mac is a charming but slight arcade conversion, but Congo’s Caper and Lost in the Tropics are the real draw, and rewind, save states, and Boss Rush make all three easy to dip into on Switch 2.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Developer: Red Art Studios (Data East originals)
Release date: 29 October 2026 (Digital), 2027 (Physical)
Platform: Switch (reviewed), Switch 2, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC

I always preferred Bonk!'s oddball platforming and Toki's tighter, almost shooter-like design to the Joe & Mac series, but in the early ’90s, if you owned a console, you needed Data East's caveman ninja. The cavemen were daft, the dinosaurs were enormous, and the colours leapt from my old CRT. I was happy to revisit these games on Switch 2 (I'm playing the Switch edition), but I wasn’t expecting the two sequels to leave the biggest impression.

The Joe & Mac Retro Collection brings together three Data East SNES games: Joe & Mac: Caveman Ninja, Congo’s Caper, and Joe & Mac 2: Lost in the Tropics (known as Joe & Mac 3 in Japan). They’re all variations on the same prehistoric platforming idea, but each takes it in a slightly different direction. The original is an arcade conversion, Congo’s Caper is a proper console platformer of the era, and the third game adds a small map, some exploration and the option to build a camp and woo cave girls. Well, you didn’t get that in Toki.

The original Joe & Mac is the simplest of the bunch. You run, jump and fling weapons at dinosaurs and other prehistoric nasties, moving through colourful stages until you reach the next boss. It’s straightforward arcade stuff, and the loose animation makes it easy to forgive the old-school frustrations like sudden deaths, enemies respawning just off-screen, and forced weapon pick-ups that make life harder (does anyone really like the stone wheel throwables?).

The dinosaur designs are still adorable. Their eyes bulge when they’re hit, and their little bodies wobble, and even getting battered by one is funny to watch. The bosses, though, rarely offer much of a challenge, and the action doesn’t have the staying power of the games that follow.

Congo’s Caper is where things get more interesting. Its core design has more in common with Sonic the Hedgehog and Kid Chameleon than the arcade original, with greater emphasis on platforming, exploration, and finding things tucked away off the main route. Hidden rooms and collectables give you a reason to poke around, and the climbable vines that grow up the screen are a lovely bit of old-school design. Take the easy route, or hang around while the vines grow and see how far up you can get?

Then there’s Joe & Mac 2: Lost in the Tropics (erm, 3?), which returns to the original's action-platform template but takes it a step further. There’s a map, you choose which levels to tackle, and between bouts of dinosaur-bashing you can build a camp and woo cave girls by spending collected stone coins on flowers. It’s a much bigger game than the original, with a bolder art direction and more to do than just reach the end of a stage.

I can’t escape the feeling that this one owes something to Toki. The bigger pixel designs and seed-spitting combat remind me of that game’s mix of shooting and traversal. The ground shifts beneath your ape’s weight, ice makes him slide, and the levels offer more than just platforms and enemies to clear. It borrows from a good source, and the extra ideas work.

Having all three together lets you watch the series work through those ideas. The first game nails the basic formula; Congo’s Caper makes platforming the main thing in a very 90s console-specific way – more complex levels, secrets, power upgrades, collectables – and Lost in the Tropics brings the two together with some exploration and more ways to dispatch dinosaurs. Most people will remember the original, but the sequels have more legs, more ideas and, in 2026, more playability.

The art is what keeps me coming back, and honestly, it's what I loved about these games back in the '90s. These games are bright, chunky, and full of character, with exaggerated 16-bit animation that makes everything feel slightly over-the-top and vibrant. The bosses show it off best in their exaggerated, head-heavy designs and attack methods: a T-Rex spits its caveman lunch, and a diplodocus spurts water jets.

The new Boss Rush mode lets you take on the bosses from all three games in succession. The later games offer more variety, and it’s a good excuse to enjoy the designs without replaying entire levels. I particularly like how Lost in the Tropics teases its bosses before you fight them. The triceratops that smashes through an ice wall piece by piece is wonderfully dramatic. The effect is simple, but the build-up makes the reveal land.

Red Art Games has included the modern conveniences you’d hope for. Rewind rescues you when an old platformer catches you out, and save states mean you don’t have to replay the same sections to get back to where you were. It also offers an optional CRT filter and a selection of custom frames, which smooth out the old pixels like the TVs would.

There’s some real preservation work here. You get the Western releases alongside the Japanese editions, including the uncensored Japanese version of Caveman Ninja, which will interest anyone curious about how these games were presented in different markets.

The virtual unboxing lets you look over the original SNES boxes, cartridges and manuals, and an art gallery gathers concept designs and character sketches. You don’t get the feel of a real manual, as the physical editions will, due for release in 2027, but you can flick through the originals.

I’d have liked more on the people who made these games, perhaps interviews or oral histories. Digital Eclipse has shown how much richer a retro collection can be when it pairs development stories with the artwork and packaging, as I found in the recent Toy Toy Story: Retro Roundup! + Toy Story 3 Complete Edition. Here, I wanted to know more about the artists behind those bulging dinosaur eyes and how the games changed from one entry to the next, but I only had the sketches to look at.

This collection is better than I expected. Joe & Mac: Caveman Ninja is still a charming slice of early-’90s arcade platforming, though it shows its age. Congo’s Caper is more inventive and rewards exploration but feels like a very of its time platformer, while Lost in the Tropics takes the series somewhere bigger and more involved.

The lack of developer interviews is a missed opportunity, and these are still old platformers with all the quirks that entails. But rewind, save states, and Boss Rush give them new life, and the virtual packaging and art gallery show that someone cares about preserving them properly.
If you remember playing Joe & Mac in the ’90s, you'll find plenty here. If you don’t, the two sequels might surprise you, and that's why I’d recommend it.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World.
