items.title: ‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care laws
paragraphs: The federal government wants to ban AI chatbots which seek to create “emotional intimacy” after prime minister Anthony Albanese raised the alarm in a heartfelt speech about children treating these agents as their “best friend”.

But Labor is coming under increasing pressure to empower the telecommunications ombudsman to become a watchdog for social media and AI to give Australians an external complaints mechanism and allow the “naming and shaming” of big tech.

The digital duty of care bill passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday and will be debated by the Senate in coming weeks. The government hopes to pass the bill by the end of 2026, but its pathway through the upper house remains unclear. The Greens support the bill, while the Coalition has said it will not vote for it, though Labor still appears keen to win the opposition’s support and remains open to amendments.

The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. It would also require social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, has suggested content that that promotes misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured by the laws. On Wednesday, the government accepted amendments from crossbencher Kate Chaney which would add certain AI chatbot activity to the list of harms, requiring platforms to ban “material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child’s dependence on it in place of human relationships”.

In an emotional address on Tuesday night, where he again implored the Coalition to consider voting for the bill, Albanese said: “the stories we hear about people identifying a chatbot, a non-person as their best friend, should be a huge wake up call for every member of this parliament to be prepared to act.”

The opposition voted against the bill in the House, alongside One Nation. Political opponents have accused Labor of an “Orwellian” system of “censorship” and of seeking to influence conversations online – claims Wells strongly denied.
“If they really care, the test is simple here, they should bring an amendment, not a slogan to ‘kill the bill’,” Wells told ABC radio on Wednesday.

Another Chaney amendment accepted by Labor would require the algorithm opt-out features to be “accessible, easy to use” and “prominently available” on platforms, amid concerns that social media firms may offer only small or hard-to-find features.

The bill now moves to the Senate, where the Greens have set up an inquiry to probe the laws due to report back in late November. Senator Sarah Hanson-Young backed a digital duty of care, calling for the government’s legislation to be strengthened. The Greens want Australians to have the right to pursue private legal action against platforms and for penalties to be increased.
“Australians also need an external complaints pathway, free from the profit-driven whims of big tech’s content moderation,” she said.

Independent MP Sophie Scamps had proposed changes to the bill to expand the remit of the telecommunications industry ombudsman. She said such a watchdog – which does not currently exist for big tech – would allow ordinary social media users to seek remedies to their accounts being hacked or inaccessible, including compensation, and investigate broader issues to name and shame companies behaving badly.
Labor did not accept this amendment in the lower house and Wells declined to voice support for such an idea, but the Greens will push for such a reform in their Senate negotiations.

The telecommunications industry ombudsman, Cynthia Gebert, said her office would be well placed to carry out such a role for big tech. She said such roles were funded by the industries they regulate and that expanding its remit could be financed by big tech.

“There are some real strengths in the DDOC [digital duty of care] because it’s putting the onus on platforms to make things safe … but I think the area that needs to be strengthened is giving people somewhere to go if they can’t get their complaints resolved with the platform,” Gebert said.
“It risks leaving Australians in the safe place they are now, where they get automated responses or escalation procedures that don’t go anywhere.”
Gebert said the government should make it mandatory for big tech to be part of an ombudsman scheme, saying it would “hold industry to account and drive system improvement”.
“[The telecommunications industry ombudsman] can help with your Telstra account, but we can’t help with your Gmail account. Consumers come to us sometimes and ask, ‘why this, not that?’,” she said.
“We want to help but don’t have the powers to do so now.”

items.title: Neil Young again sues Trump campaign for playing Rockin' in the Free World at rally
paragraphs: Rock veteran Neil Young has filed a $10m lawsuit against a fundraising committee that supports US President Donald Trump, citing "unauthorised" use of his 1989 song Rockin' in the Free World.

The Canadian-American star alleges that the Trump 47 Committee infringed on his copyright when it played the song before Trump took the stage at a 12 October rally in Ohio. Playing the song amounts to an "unauthorised public performance", the lawsuit says.
The singer-songwriter sued the Trump re-election campaign in 2020 over its use of the same song and Devil's Sidewalk. Young said the parties settled the matter shortly thereafter.
The BBC has contacted the Republican National Committee for comment.
The White House referred the BBC to the Republican National Committee for comment.
Through his company Silver Fiddle Music, Young alleges that the song was played without a license or Young's permission at a political event in Youngstown, Ohio on 12 October.
In the US, music used at campaign rallies often requires a public performance licence for it to be played for an audience, even if a campaign has already purchased a legal copy of the recording.

According to US Congress, because sound recordings do not have a general public-performance right, permission is only needed from the musical-work copyright holders, which can be obtained directly from the copyright holders themselves or through performing rights organisations.

The five-page federal lawsuit says that Trump "was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required license". It also says the song has been played "numerous times at other rallies".

The Grammy Award winner, 80, who has strongly opposed Trump's politics, characterises the song as "a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten".
Young says that the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for".
In 2020, Young sued Trump's re-election campaign for copyright infringement over the same song, as well as Devil's Sidewalk.
The new lawsuit claims that the campaign, at the time, "asserted no defence and immediately settled shortly after it was served", promising to never use the song without permission again.
Young posted about the lawsuit on his website on Tuesday, thanking Trump for coming to so many of his shows in the 1980s and 1990s, but stopped short of allowing him to play his music.
"I am sorry it came to this, but money and transactions are something you understand," he wrote.
Young, The Rolling Stones, Rihanna, Adele, REM and the estate of Prince have previously criticised the president for using their music at campaign events.

items.title: 'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones
paragraphs: Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.
Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.
Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.
Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.
While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.
Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.
"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.
Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?
One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.
The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.
Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.
Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.
Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.
For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.
He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – expect that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.
"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"
The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.
"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

items.title: Metropolis: more than four decades of street photography – in pictures
paragraphs: Metropolis: Street Photography 1985–2025 transitions from the tough, film-noir streets of 1980s New York, to the time surrounding the fall of the Berlin Wall, to the modern, colour-saturated, hard-shadowed geometry of contemporary Australian streets. Spanning classic monochrome grit and vivid colour abstraction, this remarkable collection examines how photographers have documented the relentless energy of our ever-changing cities. Ultimately, it is a celebration of the unscripted characters, strange encounters and the absurd comedy that unfolds when people share public space. On now until 17 November at The Photographic Gallery, Sydney Continue reading...

items.title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
paragraphs: AI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.

Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.

The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.

All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.
The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.

Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”

The DHSC excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. Keir Starmer’s Labour government inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.
Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.

“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.
“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”
Azzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.

“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.

“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”
The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.
A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.
“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.
“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”

items.title: UN official says North Korea’s human rights situation has not improved over past decade
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

North Korea’s human rights situation has not improved over the past decade and has deteriorated significantly in some key areas, including the use of the death penalty, a senior U.N. human rights official told VOA.

James Heenan, representative of the U.N. Human Rights Office in Seoul, said concerns persist over political prison camps, restrictions on movement, and access to food and health care. “Our assessment is that the situation, particularly over the last decade, has overall not improved,” Heenan said during an October 22 interview in Washington. “In some key respects, it’s degraded significantly.”
He pointed to increases in both executions and the number of offenses punishable by death as a major concern.

Heenan also stressed the urgency of resolving longstanding enforced disappearance cases involving South Koreans, Japanese and citizens of other countries. Victims, relatives and alleged perpetrators are aging, narrowing the time available to establish what happened and pursue justice, he said.

He noted some anecdotal indications of reduced ill-treatment in detention, including accounts that central authorities had instructed personnel not to beat detainees. But he cautioned that such limited signs of improvement did not change the broader assessment.
Heenan also warned that repeatedly publishing the identities of the two North Korean prisoners of war held in Ukraine could increase risks to them and their relatives.
Even if they have been revealed before, it doesn’t allow people to reveal them again,” he said.
In North Korea, people perceived as having broken the law can face harsh punishment and that can extend to their families, Heenan said.
Asked about reports that the prisoners had been transferred from Ukraine to South Korea, Heenan said his office did not know the terms of the transfer agreement and had no access to the men.
“What I’ve said is based on public press reports,” he said.
He called for privacy protections and appropriate assistance, including mental health and psychosocial support.
“Their well-being needs to be the center of the story,” he said.

Heenan also spoke to VOA about the issue of North Koreans who have escaped to China and are being forcibly returned to North Korea. He said authorities must first assess whether anyone repatriated could risk abuse or torture upon returning to North Korea.

The U.N. Convention Against Torture, which China ratified forbids returning anyone to a country where they could face a risk of torture. The rule is called "non-refoulement." China considers North Koreans who cross its border as economic migrants and returns them as part of an agreement with Pyongyang. Critics say this allows China to ignore its legal obligations against refoulment.
U.N. reporting has documented particularly severe punishment for returnees who expressed interest in reaching South Korea, embraced Christianity or had contact with Christian pastors.
Heenan said tighter border controls had reduced departures from North Korea, making conditions inside the country more difficult to assess.

He also raised concerns about South Koreans detained in North Korea, citing cases where they are denied consular access. He said there are also concerns about judicial fairness and the methods used to obtain evidence supporting convictions.

Heenan said that going forward it is necessary to set up a system that will hold North Korean officials accountable for abuses. He said that should include criminal trials and civil proceedings, as well as recognition of victims, truth-telling, compensation, and psychological support.

His office maintains a central repository database containing thousands of potential crimes in North Korea that could someday be used as evidence in future trials. Some information could be shared with countries that have appropriate jurisdiction over crimes committed abroad, he said.
Until those trials can happen, Hennan said the work of collecting and preserving evidence must continue. “It is laborious work,” he said. “But it’s a long-term goal.”

items.title: UN: Large-scale return of Afghan refugees strains Afghan economy
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
The return of millions of Afghan refugees from Iran and Pakistan has put pressure on the Afghan economy, according to the United Nations.
The United Nations Development Program in Afghanistan said Tuesday in a post on X that the large-scale return of Afghans has added “pressure on jobs, essential services and infrastructure.”
The U.N. said that nearly 1.3 million Afghans have returned, including those deported, from Pakistan and Iran, the two countries hosting most of Afghan refugees, to Afghanistan, so far in 2026.
UNDP adds that between 2023 and 2025, about 4.9 million Afghans returned to the country.

Even with the millions of returns, the U.N. says that 4.4 million Afghans are still living in Iran, including 1.4 million undocumented Afghans. About 1.6 million Afghans live in Pakistan including an estimated 159 thousand undocumented Afghans.
The U.N. said that “policy changes and economic pressures” in host countries have led to large-scale deportations and returns of Afghans.
The returns have further burdened vulnerable communities and essential services, according to the U.N.
The World Food Program said about 19.2 million people face acute food insecurity, while 4 million women and children are expected to suffer from malnutrition in 2027.

Afghan returnees are “with few or no resources, leaving them to settle in remote mountainous areas far from major roads and essential services. They live in makeshift shelters, often just tents under the scorching sun or on bare stones, with no access to clean water, food, or even basic shelter,” said the UNHCR. “Healthcare is out of reach, and many lack even the simplest identification documents, leaving them vulnerable and invisible in the margins of society.

Mohammad Bashir Doodyal, a former economics professor at Kabul University, told VOA that poverty, a lack of job opportunities and presence of diseases could pose major challenges to the integration of returnees into Afghan society.
“It is the responsibility of governments to plan ... to address these issues,” said Doodyal, adding that “it looks there are no such plans in place.”
He added that Afghanistan would need to improve its relations with neighboring countries and the international community to attract domestic and foreign investment needed to strengthen the economy.
“Afghanistan must emerge from isolation and have a government that the international community can trust and work with,” Doodyal said.

Khan Jan Alokozay, president of the Afghan chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told VOA that neither the government nor the private sector has the capacity to absorb millions of Afghans at once.

items.title: Tech Life
paragraphs: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK.

A week ago, few outside of the tech world had heard of PHP. Now, after vulnerabilities were discovered, it’s an acronym many more of us are familiar with. items.title: Manual's camera shop in New York is imbued with "philosophy of skate shop"
paragraphs: Design-build studio Protean Practice and camera company Manual have collaborated on the brand’s first storefront and photo lab, outfitting a Chinatown shop with plywood seating, metallic finishes and baby-pink accents.

Manual founder Malcolm Dia told Dezeen that creating a downtown gathering spot for the next generation of photographers drove the design. It is a space where they can “pull up in the morning, grab a camera, go live your life, and then come back, get it developed and hang out”.

“We thought of it as making us home base for photographers,” said Dia. “[There is] a wall of product and ways to inspire yourself, ways to interact, and then the other half is an area to hang out and chill. It’s kind of like the philosophy of a skate shop.”

Founded in 2017, Manual produces a pocket-sized, translucent digital camera called Holo, disposable cameras and film. It initially operated out of pop-ups before opening its Chinatown store this past month.

The Manual Photo Lab is the brand’s first permanent brick-and-mortar shop and also operates as a film processing lab. It’s located along Allen Street in a former point-of-sale (POS) supply store, with a retail space towards the front and a pink curtain that conceals the shop’s operations at the back.

The facade is floor-to-ceiling glass, with a translucent polycarbonate upper bulkhead that exposes the 1800s brickwork from storefronts past, as well as the shop’s name displayed in straightforward black font.

Protean Practice co-founder Saji Abu-Gold told Dezeen that the choice of polycarbonate material on the facade of the building and the interior ceiling was partially informed by Holo’s coloured plastic shell, which exposes its underworkings, such as the camera’s battery.

The studio attempted to save elements of the original signage instead of a full replacement. It stripped the covering, but maintained the structural skeleton, and infilled it with the polycarbonate sheathing.
It also restored a fluorescent light that was behind the original bulkhead.

“[When] we started to take off the layers of signage and the giant neon sign that was above, we realized that the frame, while a bit uneven, had a really nice structural skeletal shape to it underneath all the layers of vinyl and signage that people had put,” said Abu-Gold.
“We finished installation at night, and it had this refraction effect that is similar to the flashlight coming through the plastic of the Holo camera, so it ended up working out really well.”

To encourage gathering, the team created a large, multi-level Baltic birch seating unit that takes up most of the left side of the store. Prints curated by talent agency Silvertooth Agency and a commissioned painting by artist Leon Xu were arranged around the unit for the shop’s opening.
Abu-Gold said the unit was partially informed by the work of American designers Ward Bennett and Joe D’Urso.
“At the front, we met the platform with the lip of the window edge, which is something [D’Urso] did often, and then [we] brought up the tiers further throughout the store,” said Abu-Gold.
The lower lip was created for visitors “to sit on the floor comfortably without it being an actual floor”, while the upper level “encourages people to stay awhile”.
Cold-rolled steel wall panels line the shop on either side. An oversized, backlit steel pegboard by designer and fabricator Ian Chapin was cut into one along the entrance, which holds product.
Towards the back of the store, a column of custom aluminium shelving displays zines and other merchandise, while plywood, pink and steel speakers by Miami studio Lupo hang in the corners.

A baby-pink curtain lines the back wall beyond a retail counter, and conceals Manual’s operations. Visitors can drop off film at the counter, and Manual couriers it to a family-owned shop and longtime partner in Flatbush for processing.

Dia said the shop is geared towards people picking up a camera or film for the first time, and that the store is not trying to “take any business away” from other long-standing photo labs in the area such as Sammy Photo Lab and Elize Digital – the latter recently went viral for its Passport pictures.

“A big reason why I wanted to make the stores was to make it for the kids who come down the street and pick up their digital camera or roll of film for the very first time, and we want to be that for them, the next generation,” he said.
Elsewhere in Chinatown, architecture studio Spaced Agency recently designed a street-level expansion to long-standing Chinese restaurant Wo Hop, while a much-contested jail is now under construction.

Protean Practice operates between Los Angeles, New York City and London and was founded in 2022 by apparel designer Saji Abu-Gold and photographer Steven Traylor. The studio works across residential and retail projects, with a focus on low-emission, local material sourcing and maintaining existing site conditions where possible.
Design: Saji Abu-GoldCreative direction: ManualConstruction lead: Agim LamajMillwork collaborator: Matthew AvolettaStainless peg wall: Ian ChapinSound system: Lupo

items.title: The Museum of the American Revolution in Philadelphia now speaks Ukrainian
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
The Museum of the American Revolution in Philadelphia has become the fifth institution in the United States to introduce Ukrainian-language audio guides.

"The Museum of the American Revolution allows people from around the world in 2026 to understand and connect with the people and events of 1776 during the American Revolution, and delivers narratives about the immense complexity, diversity, and uncertainty that the Revolutionary generation faced," said Tyler Putman, senior manager of gallery interpretation.

"To be able to offer Ukrainians and Ukrainian speakers a resource in their own language in order to explore The Declaration's Journey, and the chance to better understand how independence movements across time and space inform each other and connect people from disparate corners of the world, is a great honor for our institution," added Putman during the official presentation of the audio guide, held at the museum on October 22.

The exhibition The Declaration’s Journey, which explores the influence of the U.S. Declaration of Independence on historical events over the past 250 years, includes Ukraine’s Declaration of Independence, displayed alongside declarations from other nations.

This was part of the initiative launched in 2019 by Ukraine’s first lady, Olena Zelenska, who continues to introduce Ukrainian-language audio guides at leading cultural and historical landmarks around the world.

“For Ukrainians living far from home, hearing their native language in a place like this museum is a meaningful connection to their roots. The Ukrainian language is also a way for us to engage as equals through culture, art, and history,” said Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in the United States, during his remarks at the museum.

“The Ukrainian language is an essential part of our national identity and a powerful expression of our resilience, dignity, and freedom. For centuries, Russia has sought to suppress our language and erase our cultural identity. Preserving our language and sharing our history are essential to protecting Ukraine’s identity,” he said.
Iryna Mazur, honorary consul of Ukraine in Philadelphia, and president of the Ukrainian Federation of America, helped bring the audio guide to the Museum of the American Revolution.

Such guides are now available in 59 countries worldwide. Visitors can hear Ukrainian at such renowned sites as the Palace of Versailles, the Colosseum, the Tower of London, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.

items.title: ACOTAR fans put real life on hold for latest release
paragraphs: As I arrive at Waterstones in York shortly before 08:00, there is already a queue forming outside the bookshop.
Fans of Sarah J Maas's bestselling A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series are waiting eagerly to get their hands on the latest instalment.
Among them is Olivia Bray, 28, who has spent more than a decade immersed in the American author's fantasy world.
For Bray, the appeal goes beyond magic, romance and fantastical kingdoms. It is the feminism running through Maas's books that has kept her coming back.

And with the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, Bray is prepared to put real life on hold, having booked an entire week off work to give herself time to recover from whatever awaits her between the covers.
"I'll be done [with reading] by tomorrow," she said. "I've just got the whole week off in case it's traumatising."
Set in the fictional world of Prythian, the series has amassed millions of fans across the world.
The series follows Feyre Archeron, a young huntress drawn into the dangerous world of the fae, where she navigates political intrigue, war and romance.

There have been five books so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021).
A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in the best-selling series, was released on Tuesday - five years after fans last heard from the characters.
Another ACOTAR fan, 22-year-old Abigail Wright, hoped to finish the book on release day, which coincided with her day off, before returning to work.
She said the books were her "gateway back into reading" aged 19.
Like Bray, Wright believed the recurring theme of female empowerment was a key part of its appeal.
"I think it's so popular because, yes, the romantic side of it is very good, but the strong women you see in the books are just a way to make other young women feel really empowered," said Wright.

"It just gives them a sense of power and [makes them] see you can start from nothing, like Feyre does, and just make your way up… you don't need a man to do all these things for you, you have the power to do anything you want to do."

Gabriella Booth, 29, was introduced to the series in 2013, but attributes ACOTAR's explosion in popularity to both the pandemic and "BookTok" - a TikTok community dedicated to sharing what people are reading and writing.
"The characters in general are so easy to read about. You can relate in different parts to a lot of them, I find," said Booth.

"For me, I love the fantasy world - that's something I've loved reading growing up. So, to have that combined with the romance side of everything... there's something that's just so exciting to read about."
Booth has previously taken time off work to read new releases and plans to do so when the seventh ACOTAR book is published in January.
However, on this occasion, she hopes to finish A Court of Splintered Harmony after work.

Alice Boyce, a bookseller at Topping and Company Booksellers on Museum Street in York, said ACOTAR fans had made their way straight up to the science-fiction area of the store as soon as doors opened at 09:00.
"People are really enthusiastic; we've had emails saying, 'can you put a copy aside for me?', and last night we had people asking to put it on pre-order."
An ACOTAR fan herself, 26-year-old Boyce said she felt she could truly disconnect when she read the books.
"You can dive into books and just escape a little bit," she added.
Events were held across the UK, including in Wolverhampton and Northern Ireland, to mark the new book's release, with Waterstones on York's Coney Street hosting its first ever midnight release event.
Eighty ACOTAR fans, some of whom were dressed as their favourite characters, attended the event, while 100 members of the fandom flocked to a party in Wolverhampton.
Organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, told the BBC people were "ecstatic" when the book was finally released.
"The community was just lovely, it was so nice to see everybody come together and fan-girl over a book," Fellows said.
Fellows, who booked the day off work to read the book, said she was already through the first chapter.
"It sounds like it's going to be incredible", she said.

items.title: Unnamed celebrity accused of 'inappropriate sexual activities', court hears
paragraphs: A celebrity has asked the High Court to prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations that he abused his status for many years to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".
The unnamed celebrity is seeking an injunction, and his legal team told the first day of a trial on Tuesday that any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself.
They told the court that his drastic reaction was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".
The man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them", the court heard.

The legal team for ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) told the court that the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be mitigated and there was no proper basis "to restrain the publication of public interest journalism".

A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".
The judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said there was "significant public interest" in the proceedings and that "this is a difficult and important case".
He added: "The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions."
Nicklin will not determine the truth or accuracy of the allegations, only whether they can be published.
He also urged the press and public not to speculate about the identity of the man, who is referred to in court as PPT.

"The existence of online speculation, however confidently expressed or widely repeated, does not authorise anyone to identify, or purport authoritatively to identify, PPT in connection with these proceedings," he said.
"Nor does repetition transform speculation into established fact."
Sara Mansoori KC, representing the man, told the court that any publication "would have a potentially fatal impact".
The barrister told the court: "The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life."

She said the man had made a suicide attempt after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his response to the allegations, and later absconded from hospital and attempted suicide for a second time.
She added in written submissions: "This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur.

"The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple - now more than 10 - doctors."
Mansoori also said the man "has no intention of returning to public life".

Gavin Millar KC, for ITN and GNM, said in written submissions that "numerous allegations" had been gathered during "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a "strong" public interest in publishing them.
He said reporters had spoken to more than 100 people, and that the resulting allegations "indicated a pattern of behaviour".
Millar later said many of the women "have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result".

He added that while the state may have a responsibility to protect life, applying that principle to this case would require the state to intervene in "lawful journalistic activities" to prevent "an autonomous act by the claimant himself".
The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

items.title: "Jagged" New York house is Aston Martin's first US residence
paragraphs: Automotive company Aston Martin has collaborated with US studio S3 Architecture for the Sylvan Rock residential compound in Upstate New York, conforming the metal roofline to the outcroppings of stone on the site.
Located in the town of Red Hook, Sylvan Rock features a faceted, black-metal roofline that angles with the house, which was built to follow the site’s slope.
At the low end, the roof meets the ground, covering a walkway that leads to the primary entrance.
“When designing, we always let the land speak first and respond to it,” said S3 Architecture partner Christopher Dierig.
“The roofline mimics the jagged edges of the rock ledge reaching down into the earth, as if the home is born of and launching from the landscape,” Dierig continued.
A stairway leads up from the lower entrance into the primary spaces of the house, which has two storeys on top of the outcropping.
Also on the lower level is a garage that forms a plinth for one of two swimming pool areas. Part of the garage was carved into the rockspace and the studio referred to it as “subterranean”.
The main, elevated body of the residence has glass walls interspersed with black metal panelling. Four bedrooms and five bathrooms are spread over this space.
Living and dining spaces are located on the ground plane, in line with the pool areas. A glass bridge connects an auxiliary spa and sauna space.
Luxury wood finishes and stone filter through the interiors, which are mostly monotone.
A floating staircase sits in the middle of the plan and provides access to the upper level, which holds the bedroom suites and features balconies that look out into the wooded landscape.
Wooden ceilings and beams lighten up the space and multiple fireplaces were included in the living spaces, including in the primary suite upstairs.
These interior spaces were designed by the Aston Martin team and also feature one-of-a-kind custom furniture by the brand.

Certain elements have direct reference to the company’s branding, including the brand’s lattice motif covering the wine storage in the primary lounge and a movie theatre that includes seating reminiscent of automobile seats.
The site also includes guest residences, a pavilion and a treehouse. The residences feature similar metal roofs and exteriors.
The house is one of two branded residences by Aston Martin planned throughout the world, with the other located in Japan.
It follows a trend of automotive brands entering the architecture field, directly designing residences and even skyscrapers, especially in the US.
For example, Bugatti unveiled a branded skyscraper design for Miami last month. Aston Martin completed its own skyscraper in Miami in 2024.
Photography by Will Nainis of Sundae Spaces

items.title: Anthropic accelerates – for the rest of us, the speed of growth spells precarity
paragraphs: Today in tech, we’re discussing Anthropic’s astronomic growth, how a settlement over social media safety dented Meta’s revenue, and Lula’s accusations of interference against Meta.

Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on the US stock market on Monday, ahead of what it slated to be one of the biggest debuts in financial history. The company withheld a valuation from its filing with US financial regulators, but investors and analysts are valuing the AI firm at north of $1.5tn.

The numbers are jaw-dropping and speak to the speed of the AI boom. Anthropic was founded in 2021. That’s only five years ago, yet already it has grown to a valuation bigger than 98% of the top companies on the US stock market.

Anthropic detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (a yearly increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.
Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026, mostly due to a one-time $72.4bn charge. It lost $36bn the year prior.

Anthropic’s initial public offering will rock the US stock market and probably global markets as well. The infusion of at least a trillion dollars in value is likely to influence investor appetites for every kind of technology stock. That a company of that magnitude can be spun up in five years speaks to the breakneck pace of AI development and financing. Despite calls to slow down from Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, the artificial intelligence industry is still defined by a careening intensity that’s taking the world’s finances along for the ride.
Such rapid growth demonstrates an upside for company founders for now. They can build a business that creates life-changing, globe-spanning wealth in just half a decade.

For the rest of us, the speed of growth spells precarity. Anthropic, a company that could determine the direction of the entire US economy, is going public before a baby born in its founding year has started kindergarten.
Settlements over the safety of social networks are growing so large that Meta is reporting significant drags on its business.
In August, the biggest social media company in the world agreed to a $17bn settlement with dozens of state attorneys general to put claims it had endangered children to rest without admitting guilt.

In a quarterly earnings report last week, issued the same afternoon as a judge ordered the company to pay the state of New Mexico $25bn, Meta reported net income significantly below Wall Street analysts’ expectations because of a payment towards the settlement with attorneys general, this one $9.9bn.

The dent in Meta’s business is a sign that child safety activists are succeeding. In the Los Angeles social media addiction lawsuit that took place earlier this year, lawyers for the plaintiff made it clear they’re intent on making it untenable for Meta to operate the current version of Instagram. They want to render endangering children, which they believe Meta is doing, too expensive to continue. They hope to push the company to the point where business as usual is untenable because of the financial risks of safety.
Activists can’t celebrate yet, though. Despite the hefty payments, Meta still reported a 26% increase in quarterly revenue up to $64.6bn.

items.title: ‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film
paragraphs: Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.
Having criticised the hit movie in the summer, the tycoon said he would use Grok Imagine to make a “historically accurate” adaptation.
The initial results have been released on X in the form of a seven-minute episode made in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup.
Musk had objected to Nolan’s casting choices – such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion.
The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “full-length movie” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes.

The first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy. He then sails from Ithaca, his home island, with his men crying out for “vengeance” before they make land and start fighting.
The episode ends after 10 years of conflict, with Odysseus holding, ominously, a wooden figurine of a horse.

Xavier Collins, the co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the first episode was made in less than two weeks with a creative team of three, including the US-based director Dev Walker. It is understood to have cost tens of thousands of dollars. Nolan’s version cost $250m (£188m) and was shot in multiple locations over 91 days with a vast crew. It has made $1.8bn at the box office.
Despite Musk’s criticisms of Nolan’s film, the creative team behind the latest take on Homer are supporters of the summer blockbuster.

Collins said he was a “huge fan” and told the Guardian: “We were not given any direction to make it [Musk’s version] anti-woke or anything like that. We were given the opportunity by one of the world’s best frontier labs to work on one of the best stories ever told.
“The brief was ‘help us understand the technology, where it’s strong, where it could use improvement’.”

Peter Bradshaw’s review in the Guardian gave it one star, saying: “Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver.”

The episode on the Grok Imagine X account has received 7.3m views and some harsh feedback, with a reviewer in the Telegraph saying: “You can feel your eyeballs twitch as it unfolds in all its sloppy gruesomeness.”
Collins said Wonder aimed to make the next episode an improvement on the first and would address criticism, including the historical accuracy of its boats and rapid pacing.

“We are going to take a look at all of the comments and all of the things we could have done better and see if we can improve it. The goal is that the next episode we make is radically better than the last,” he said.
Wonder has also worked with Google DeepMind to produce an AI-generated video for the Lewis Capaldi track Something in the Heavens.

items.title: Will a new strategy help protect Northern Ireland's nature?
paragraphs: Agriculture and environment correspondent, BBC News NI
A new strategy to restore and enhance protection for nature in Northern Ireland has been launched by the agriculture and environment minister.
About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats
Minister Andrew Muir said supporting nature was "not just a nice thing to do", but "a moral obligation to future generations".
But the minister acknowledged that money would be needed to address the challenges.
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status
The strategy highlights the importance of nature as providing the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe.
Muir said nature must be put "back at the heart of everything we do, because when nature thrives, people flourish.
"It is essential to a strong economy, healthier communities and a more resilient Northern Ireland.
"With so much of our natural world lost, we must protect what remains, restore what has been damaged and create new habitats at scale."
Many places in Northern Ireland support rare or threatened plants, animals and habitats.
They can be legally designated to help ensure better management and protection of those species.

There are hundreds of such designated sites across Northern Ireland, covering around 10% of the land and 38% of coastal waters - classed as Areas of Special Scientific Interest; Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) which have international biodiversity importance; Ramsar Sites which cover wetlands of international importance; Special Protection Areas (SPAs); and Marine Conservation Zones (MCZs).
That should lead to work to protect the species and habitats they have been designated for.
But the Office for Environmental Protection found not enough sites are being designated and the condition of those that have been is worsening.
The number of sites that were in favourable condition dropped from 61.7% in 2008, to 51.5% in 2024.
It is now investigating how those sites are being managed, external by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, after it found implementation of the designation fell short.
Northern Ireland is one of the most nature-depleted areas in the world, according to the 2023 State of Nature Report.
It found 12% of species here are under threat of extinction, and the number of flowering plants had declined by 14% since 1970.

The Nature Recovery Strategy identifies six external pressures affecting nature and biodiversity - invasive species; climate change; human impact through inappropriate development; land and sea-use change; increased intensive farming; pollution.
It says these must all be addressed effectively to allow nature to thrive.

items.title: This AI billboard might be too ballsy for its own good
paragraphs: Recently, billboard ads have been getting daring. From brands ditching their logos to wild guerrilla marketing, we've seen some real out-of-the-box thinking, but this latest ad from AI company Notion might be the most gutsy yet.

Placing itself shoulder to shoulder with the competition, Notion's confident ad proves that it stands out against its rivals. Dividing critics with its bold and minimalist billboard design, the ad proves that creative bravery is a priceless tool for standing out in a crowded market.
i can’t even tell who the billboard is for 😭 https://t.co/jclLv2cdtBOctober 26, 2026

The billboard in question features a lineup of AI logos including Claude, Perplexity, Grok Bot, ChatGPT and, of course, Notion front and centre. It might seem a little barmy to place yourself among the competition in your own ad, but it's this very confidence that makes Notion's ad shine.

"As much as I hate to admit it, this is a really great ad," a user on X wrote. "No words, just app icons. There’s mystery over who paid for it. There's controversy over why certain apps should be there. It's bold and makes a statement," they added. "Super cool and smart, or super dumb?" another added.

I, for one, am in the "super cool" camp. Given that most AI logos look the same, Notion's simple letterblock logo instantly stands out against the competition. The neutral ground of the logo lineup only helps Notion to emerge among its competitors, suggesting a certain edge against the competition.

While some have criticised the billboard for being too vague, I think that's where its strength emerges. The best adverts often spark conversation, and Notion's bold billboard is not only a symbol of confidence, but a conversation prompt about where the brand belongs in the AI sphere.

items.title: Rare dinosaur skeleton goes to auction in New York with £4.5m price tag
paragraphs: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex is up for auction - with a price-tag of at least $6m (£4.5m).
Nicknamed "Jodi", the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton will be auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.

The Late Cretaceous carnivore is expected to fetch up to $9m when it goes under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed "Gus", for a record $50.1m (£37.4m) in July.
The sales comes as some in the scientific community debate whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately.
Sotheby's described "Jodi" as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".

The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science." The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.

Megan Jenkins, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".
"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jenkins said.
Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.
"Jodi" was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.

The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hall Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.

Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from "Jodi" in 2006.

The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.
The auction of "Jodi" comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.
Researchers told the BBC after the sale of "Gus" that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.

Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".

"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."
He said that the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.
Responding to today's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that "Jodi" could disappear from public view.

"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.
But Jenkins told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.

"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

items.title: Etsy's crackdown on AI slop is welcome, but it shows how far things have slipped
paragraphs: It's good to have rules. But there's only so far you can go without needlessly stating the obvious. You wouldn't, for example, expect to see signs in restaurant kitchens saying "Don't serve raw chicken". Store managers don't email their cashiers telling them to "Give customers the correct change". These things are common sense, and don't generally need to be said out loud.
So why is Etsy suddenly telling its sellers: "The photo of the product you're selling should actually be the photo of the product you're selling"?

Last week the marketplace for handmade goods made an important-sounding announcement: that every listing must now include at least one unedited photo of the actual item, shot against a real background.

It also specifically banned the use of AI image generators for patterns, recipes and instructions for customers. It's outlawed listings created by bots. And while it's still okay to see AI-generated art on Etsy, you need to be clear about that fact, so buyers know exactly what it is they're buying.
AI on Etsy: What's Allowed and What's Changing - YouTube
All of which sounds great. But I can't help feeling we never should have got to the place where any of this was necessary.

Admittedly, Etsy had to do something, because the complaints are mounting fast. Full-time creator Kara Lynne summed it up on X, writing: "I can't explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realise it's fully AI-generated, doesn't make sense, and definitely doesn't match what the finished product should be." Quite.

That's the world that AI is delivering to us. Someone spending their hard-earned money and an evening of their life on instructions that were never going to work. Multiply that by thousands of buyers and you can see how big the problem has become, both for shoppers and the majority of Etsy sellers, who are trying to do everything properly yet end up being tarred with the same brush.

So what Etsy has said does make sense, although it does make you wonder why they haven't acted sooner. Despite its folksy image, this is a company with a market cap of $7.81 billion, after all. You'd think they'd have enough cash to hire a few people to keep an eye on this stuff.

Still, at least Etsy now seems to be pulling in the same direction as much of the creative world. The company now follows Spotify pulling 50 million AI tracks, Snap keeping gen-AI content out of its recommendations and LinkedIn, well, at least adding a button to report it.

Etsy's new rules won't fix everything. But they do acknowledge what should have been obvious: that when people buy something "handmade", they want to know whether a human actually made it. Baby steps, of course, but at least they're steps in the right direction.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Scotland's recycling rates fall to lowest level in five years
paragraphs: Waste experts have warned that landfill space in Scotland is rapidly running out
Scotland environment, energy and rural affairs correspondent
Scotland's recycling rate has fallen to its lowest level in five years, according to figures from the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
The Scottish government's environmental regulator says households recycled 42.8% of waste in 2025 - down from 44.3% the previous year.
According to a roadmap set by the Scottish government in 2010, recycling rates should have hit 70% last year but are falling well short.
The share of waste processed at an incinerator remained broadly the same at 82% but the amount being diverted to landfill fell by 10%.
Recycling rates vary massively by local authority. South Ayrshire's residents recycled 55% of their waste, compared to 26% in Glasgow.
The islands have the lowest rates, with Orkney recording a figure of just 18.2%.
A total of 2.31 million tonnes of waste was created by households in 2025, which represents a fall of just 1,500 tonnes.
Recycling rates have remained similar - at about 45% - for more than a decade.
The biggest change has been seen in the way black bag waste is treated.
A rapid growth in the construction of energy-from-waste plants, which generate electricity by burning rubbish, has seen a shift away from landfill.
But this has not happened quickly enough to meet a landfill ban which was due to come in at the start of the year. It has now been effectively delayed to 2028.
The figures do not reflect a disruption to Scotland's waste management by the long-term repairs being carried out to the incinerator at Polmadie in Glasgow.
The Glasgow Recycling and Renewable Energy Centre in Glasgow was shut down in April this year, with much of the waste being diverted to other incinerators or landfill.
The centre is operated, along with a facility at Dunbar, by Viridor.
Karen MacCormick from the company says waste incineration is a greener option than landfill because it can also generate electricity.
She added: "When it's in landfill you've got the landfill gasses, you've got methane, etc.

"This is a more sustainable way of dealing with the waste, coming through an energy recovery facility, and obviously we can create something at the end of it which is low carbon energy going straight to the grid."
A deposit return scheme for bottles and cans, which has seen recycling rates increase significantly in other countries, has been repeatedly delayed.
Experts have also suggested that the lack of consistency in what is collected by local authorities across the country makes it confusing for households.
While some councils take glass at the kerbside, for example, others are forced to drop them off at bottle banks.
Research from Zero Waste Scotland also suggests that more than half of the waste placed in black bins could be recycled.
Sepa's chief scientific officer, Dr Richard Allan, says the figures highlight an "ongoing challenge" with how waste is managed.
He added: "It's clear that where waste ends up is important, but we need to focus on preventing waste in the first place and recycling more of that material when it is produced."
Kim Pratt, senior circular economy campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said there had been a "shocking decline" in recycling rates.
She said this showed that Scotland had "lost its way", with households missing the 2025 target of 70% recycling "by a mile".

"Recycling levels have stalled in Scotland since the Scottish government encouraged a new generation of waste incinerators to be built, meaning that household waste which could have been recycled is being burned instead," she said.
"The Scottish government is expected to consult on new circular economy targets this year.
"If these are to be meaningful, it must learn the lessons from the past – setting targets is the easy part, meeting them requires real commitment and planning that puts people and nature first."
The Scottish government has been approached for comment.

items.title: Büro Ziyu Zhuang designs Chinese museum cluster to "blend seamlessly" into meadow
paragraphs: Chinese architecture studio Büro Ziyu Zhuang embedded four cultural buildings, including a viewing tower and a rammed-earth workshop, into parkland in Xianning, China, to create the Zi Museum.
Located along Zishan Lake in Xianning, Hubei Province, the project comprises four public buildings designed to complement the guest houses of the Ziyouji resort on the other side of the lake.
The centrepiece of the project is the 3,000-square-metre Zi Museum, which features a multi-faceted, layered structure made from pale concrete and was organised around a central courtyard.
Büro Ziyu Zhuang (BUZZ) created three separate access points into the museum at various levels, to follow the natural elevation of the landscape.

On the ground floor, the museum has flexible gallery spaces and a garden restaurant, with a lower-level entranced located near the main traffic route to make installation setup and collection storage easier.
At the front of the museum, a path from the main building leads to a viewpoint closer to the lake.
Visitors can also go from the viewpoint into the museum’s central courtyard and straight to the viewing ramp onto the museum’s rooftop.

“Visitors who are here for nature viewing are able to bypass the interior gallery space, accessing the rooftop viewing platform directly from the outdoor park, while a different circulation was created for those who are here for the gallery exhibitions,” explained BUZZ.
“This allows serious academic exhibition and relaxed social gathering to co-exist in the same building,” it continued.
BUZZ organised the interiors of the museum as an “open labyrinth”, the studio said.
Galleries, public passages, rest and hospitality areas are intertwined to create a free-flowing viewing experience that was designed to evoke the sense of wandering in a Chinese garden.
Next to the museum sits another viewpoint, described by the studio as a “meditation tower”, which features stairs that circulate around a hollow core at its centre.
These continue underground, where they lead to a sunken courtyard wrapped in metal mesh.
The tower can be used as a viewpoint, as well as for small outdoor gatherings and exhibitions.
The third building, a rammed-earth workshop, was designed to seamlessly embed into the landscape.
Like the museum building, this also has a walking ramp, which leads up to a grass-covered rooftop while slightly revealing the entrance below.
Nearby sits the final building, a bookshop with an overhanging roof design that creates a sheltered entrance facing the main street.
It gently steps down towards the lake, where its glass facade opens up to create views over the parkland and lake.

BUZZ aimed to encourage visitors to explore freely between the four buildings. Rather than designing a set route, the studio wanted to create access to the public art space from every direction of the park.
“The overall project manifests as a continuous, open expansion of green space, which provides the flexibility needed for diverse future operations,” BUZZ said.

“There are no forced axes or rigid zoning between individual buildings; instead, they are connected organically through gentle slopes, undulating lawns, and landscaped pathways, blending seamlessly into the existing meadow,” it continued.
Büro Ziyu Zhuang was founded by architect Ziyu Zhuang in 2016. It now has offices in Beijing, Shanghai and Berlin.
The studio also recently unveiled an UFO-shaped gallery that sinks into grassland in Inner Mongolia, as well as an observatory in China that resembles a “spaceship or alien form”.

items.title: This creative agency’s website is giving me Tumblr 2000s vibes, and I’m here for it
paragraphs: I've been writing about websites since the late 2000s, when I got a job on one of Creative Bloq's forerunners, a web design title called net magazine. And believe me, in the two decades that have passed by since, I've visited a lot of creative agency websites.

If you look at a lot of anything, you tend to get snow blindness after a while. And so it's been with me. Through my tired and cynical eyes, most agency sites look like they've been built by the same person.

Looping showreel? Check? Big, bold type? Check. Meaningless waffle about how the studio is “building brands that matter” (barf). Check. An imposing contact form you sense no one human will ever be bothered to fill out? Check. I could go on, but you get the point.

That's why an email from Denver’s Bound Agency made me smile this morning. Its subject line described their new website, built by Denver studio Wunder Werkz, as "Messy, meaningful and made by humans". And it did not disappoint.

The logo is a handwritten scrawl. The navigation icons are wobbly doodles: a slice of cake, an arrow, a signpost, a camera. There are acres of white space (well, soft lilac space to be precise). And scrolling down the tiles feels like I'm flicking through a fanzine.

A collage of Dolly Parton and Tim Curry pictures, all big blonde hair and glam-rock make-up, overlaid with the words: “Pack your wigs, divas. We’re being called home.” A Juno Calypso photo of a woman in a pink heart-shaped bath, pinned with a paperclip. A Spotify playlist titled The Dregs of Summer. A Victorian paper-doll bust. If you spent any time on Tumblr in the late 2000s, it all feels very familiar.

While it's not a carbon copy of the era, many of the hallmarks are there. Found imagery, ironic captions, mixtapes, and a sense that someone’s personal taste is the whole point. Personally, I’m here for it.

So why take this approach? Bound's founder Lauren “Lolo” Butts notes that in 13 years, their website has never won them a single client. “New business almost always comes from word of mouth,” she explains. “So this revamp wasn’t about lead-gen. It was about building a beautiful, fun place that feels like the person you were already told to talk to.”

I find this super-refreshing. It frees the site from having to do lots of boring jobs. There’s no “About us” page and no list of the services the agency offers. Instead, it’s a playground. You can pull a tarot card. You can rearrange a grid that keeps changing. You can build and share a cake. You can browse an estate sale guide called Let’s Go Hunting!

Almost a year ago I wrote about a tactile rebellion against slick, synthetic design, and turns out my article headline, "Messy, meaningful and made by humans", were the very words Bound used in their email to me. Flattery will get you everywhere, as they say; but I do genuinely feel this site lives up to that promise.
Every logo, doodle and arrow on the site is in Lauren's own handwriting. And even the eyeballs subtly signal an agency willing to look clients in the eye.

You can’t prompt your way to this kind of personality in Claude; it can only come from somewhere real. And for potential clients, this site is a handy vibe check. If it holds your attention, you’re probably the kind of client they want. If it doesn’t, you’ve both saved yourselves a meeting.
In short, it's a great example of a classic design maxim: why describe your message, your point of view, when you can just show it?

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision over Israel participation
paragraphs: NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.
"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.
"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".
